speechtext: My attention has been directed to an issue of the Ottawa Free Press of Thursday, March 19, which contains what purports to be a Teport of a caucus of the Liberal-Conservative members of Parliament on Wednesday last. The statement contained in the report that a caucus of the Liberal-Conservative members was held on that day is correct, but apart, from that the report is a tissue of falsehoods from beginning to end. I would like to observe further that those who are admitted to the precincts of the House and the Press Gallery for the purpose of reporting the proceedings here have certain responsibilities as well as certain rights. Among those rights, the practice of deliberate mendacity is not included.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This Bill contains certain amendments to the -Civil Service Insurance Act, which is to be found in the Revised Statutes of Canada, chapter 18. There are two principal features to which I directed the .attention of the House upon the occasion of the consideration of the resolution preceding the Bill. The first is that the benefits of the Act are extended to female members of the service, so that the sexes are placed on an equality in that regard. The second feature is that the maximum amount of insurance is increased from $2,090 to $5,000. The other provisions of the Bill relate principally to these two features. For some time past the Civil Service have requested that legislation of this character should be enacted.

I do not happen to be
familiar with the original statute. The question has been asked, in what particulars does the status of female members of the service differ from that of the male members at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was under the impression, that my hon. friend was familiar with the statute. The Civil Service Insurance Act was enacted in 1893. Under its provisions any male member of the service occupying a permanent position is entitled to take out an insurance policy for an amount not exceeding $2,000 payable upon his death, upon paying premiums based upon fraternal society actuarial rates. The Act does not include the female members of the' service, for the treason, I presume, that at the time tne Act was passed, there may have been comparatively few females in the service. There seems no good reason why there should be a discrimination .against the ladies, and this legislation is introduced to place them upon an equality with their male fellow members of the service. The .life insurance companies generally accept risks upon the lives of women as they do upon the lives of men. At the time this Act was passed, it was considered that $2,000 would be a proper maximum amount. It is now considered that $2,000 is too small as the -maximum, having regard to the increased cost of living and other matters which I need not mention,

and that the maximum might well be increased to $5,000. The Act is administered through the Insurance Department, and therefore at comparatively little cost. According to the information I have received from the Insurance Department, the premiums paid are sufficient from an actuarial standpoint to justify the insurance granted.
I assume that taking out policies under the Act is optional with the members of the service. Do a large proportion of the service take advantage of the terms of the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: About ten per cent of those eligible have taken advantage of it.

Is it retroactive as
applying to employees who are superannuated?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That matter was brought
to my attention by my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux). The Act will not apply retroactively to those who have left the service or who have been superannuated. In the case of those now in the service who have taken out a policy for $2,000, upon passing a medical examination and paying from the date of the insurance forward, the amount of premium proper to the policy which they took out, they may increase their insurance up to a maximum of $5,000.

I had in mind those
who had been superannuated. I am under the impression that a superannuated officer is amenable to his minister, and is liable to be called back into the service to fill a temporary vacancy or for other cause. I would ask the attention of the Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) to that point. For in stance: a customs inspector has been superannuated; a vacancy occurs through death' or illness of one of the employees; has the minister authority over that superannuated officer to bring him back into the service for a time?

If an officer has been superannuated, he may be recalled to the service and re-employed, but lie is not paid a salary more than will make, with his superannuation, the salary he received before his retirement.
He can be compelled to return to the service?
Yes.

That is the point 1
was making. The retired officer being liable to be recalled, should not the increased insurance apply in his case? For, as the 
Minister of Finance says, the maximum of $2,000 which hitherto has been fixed is very low. I know that the rate of premium is moderate and the system is a good one, and I congratulate the hon. minister on the step he is taking. It seems to me that those v ho are superannuated and who, as has been shown, are amenable to their ministers, and liable to be recalled, should get the benefit of the new Act.
I may say it is very seldom that an officer is recalled.
But they are subject to be recalled.

If their health is in such
condition as to allow it, they may be recalled, but the number of those who have been recalled is very small.

What will be the
effect upon one who has severed his connection with the service?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under existing legislation regulations are made to cover that point. As a matter of practice the insured are permitted to continue their policies, but the minister has the right to pay a cash surrender value or to issue a paid-up policy for a suitable amount.

There may be fatal
objections to the point that I raise, and if so the Minister of Finance will enlighten me. But I know as a matter of fact of one man who has been superannuated, and who, I am sure, would take advantage of the new Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know that the
objection would be fatal, but I think that such insurance would be found inadvisable. In the first place, as my hon. colleague (Mr. Reid) has pointed out, services of retired officers are very seldom requisitioned. If they were to come back to the service, I think they would be entitled to the benefits of the new Act. But superannuation takes place at the age of sixty-five or later, usually nearer seventy, and for the most part men are not insurable at that age. Having regard to these considerations, I should think it would be inexpedient to extend the benefits of the Act.

This section 1 authorizes the minister to contract with ' any person to whom Part 1 of the Civil Service Superannuation and Retirement Act applies on the 1st day of April, 1914.' I am not familiar with that Act. Ms any part of the Civil Service thus excluded?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Part 1 of the Act referred to takes in the entire permanent service. The change made in this section is, my hon. friend will see, in line 13 in the words 'whether civil or'military.' Heretofore the Act has only applied to the civilian members of the service. This extends it to the headquarters staff of the militia.
Does it not apply to the outside service?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To the permanent outside service-yes.
The hon. gentleman told us the contracts were on the Friendly Society basis. Is that the H. M. table of the British Institute, or what is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The standard for fraternal societies-the National Fraternal Congress standard.
Does the Government add anything to this, or does it carry itself?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The insurance system constituted by the Insurance Act of 1906 is self-sustaining; the Government adds nothing.

I am not an expert on life insurance, but it strikes me, considering the very small number of civil servants who take advantage of this insurance, that the increase of the amount to $5,000 may disarrange the financial aspect of the matter, so that while it works out to carry itself to-day, it may not work out to carry itself under the new arrangement. I am not urging that as an objection, I am merely asking if the possibility exists.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend and I are alike in one thing at least; we both admit that we do not know a great deal about the subject of life insurance. I am advised, however, by the actuarial officer of the Insurance Department that if the amount were increased tenfold instead of more than twofold, the matter would be on precisely the same basis; that is to say, the financial aspect of it is not in any way modified or changed by the increase in the maximum amount of insurance. The premium is proportionate, of course the premium on a $5,000 policy will be two and a half times the amount of a premium upon a $2,000 policy. The Act is administered by the Superintendent of Insurance, consequently the cost is very slight indeed.

I quite understand that
the premium would be proportionate with the amount of the policy, but the security
for the policy rests upon the number of premiums as well as their amount, and if you do not have a sufficient number of premiums you are going to lose out on the payment of the policies. So, as you increase the amount of the policy, unless there is also an increase in the number of premiums, you are bound to lose out-at least, that is the way it appears to my untutored mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a sufficient number of premiums to meet the average anticipated death rate, so that no such question arises with regard to the increase of the amount from $2,000 to $5,000.

If I mistake not, the Government insurance system for its employees was inaugurated some years ago, when the superannuation system was abolished. I would like to know how many Civil Service employees have taken advantage of this insurance system. I have heard it rumoured many times during the last few months that the Government is contemplating a returii to the old system of superannuation. If that should be done, would the insurance system still be maintained?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Civil Service insurance that is now under consideration is a matter separate and apart altogether from that of superannuation. I am of the view that anything that the Government might do in the matter of instituting superannuation legislation would not have the effect of displacing the insurance system. In a general way I have had the question of superannuation under consideration, but any legislation in that regard has not yet received consideration on the part of the Government, and at the present time it would be premature to discuss it.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-section 9 amended:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This amendment is made necessary by an error which occurred in the consolidation of 1906. Section 9 of the Civil Service Insurance Act provides as follows:
Where an apportionment has been made as hereinbefore provided, and one or more of the persons in whose favour the apportionment has been made die in the lifetime of the insured, the insured may, by an instrumem in wilting endorsed on or attached to the insurance contract, declare that the shares formerly apportioned to the person so dying shall be for the benefit of the wife and children of the insured, or of one or more of them as he sees fit.

That means that he may apportion the insurance to his wife and children, or to his wife only, or to one or more of his children. Subsection 2 provides:
In default of such declaration, the shares of the persons so dying shall be for the benefit of the survivor, or, if more than one, of the survivors of the wife and children of the insured in equal shares.
Subsection 1 gives the insured the right to exclude the wife in favour of the children. By subsection 2, if one of the children dies, he must bring in the wife, although originally he may have intended to exclude the wife from the benefits of the apportionment. The amendment provides that in the event of one of the children dying the apportionment will go to the survivors of the class among whom the insured had originally apportioned, unless, of course, he expressly wishes to bring the wife in.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-section 15 amended:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I have not read the Bill, but I would like to know if it provides that in a case where there is no endorsation as to whom the policy is to be payable, the apportionment shall go to the family of the insured.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. I would direct the attention of my hon. friend to subsection 3 of section 2 of the Bill.
In the event of the death of one of the beneficiaries, are these terms embodied in the contract of insurance or in the policy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The provisions as I have read the regulations are not set out expressly in the policy, but are incorporated by reference to the Act. The beneficiaries are named in the insurance policy usually. The insurer may say simply wife and children, without expressly naming them all. If he died without making an apportionment, they would share equally under the Act.

Unless it is done as a matter of contract between the party insuring and this Government, I do not think we would have any power to legislate as to what should become of the property. That would be governed by the law of personal property in the different provinces, and I think it would be unwise for us to legislate as to what shall become of a man's personal property in any province when the provinces have their own legislation governing the personal property and real estate of the individual. I submit to the minister that it is only as a matter of contract with the Government that we should interfere. That is why 1 ask if it is the policy that we may regulate what shall become of the money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: While the individuals are not named, they are designated as his wife and children. In that way he apportions the insurance. I think I understand my hon. friend's point, that, failing the apportionment being expressly covered by the contract, the designation of the money would be controlled by the laws of the province, which, under the British North America Act, has jurisdiction in matters of property and civil rights. The actuary of the Insurance Department informs me that no question can arise, because, either by express naming or by designation, the apportionment of the money is made in the contract as a matter of contract.

I think it would be unwise for us in this Parliament to legislate as to what should become of a man's property except as it is mentioned in the policy. Beyond that I think that we might be creating a conflict of laws between the Dominion and the different provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
Public Buildings, Ottawa-New departmental buildings, and sites therefor, $1,000,000.

['During the last four
or five years we have been in the habit of passing this class of Bills, which is like the last three Bills of the Order Paper-

the Barcelona Traction, Light and Power Company, Limited, the Brazilian Traction, Light and Power Company, Limited, and the British America Nickel Corporation, Limited, which were passed last year and are being amended. This is a case where a company has letters patent in Canada. It wants to go into a foreign country to build a railway and telephone line, and to use its Canadian incorporated name. When it gets to that foreign country, it is told that, on those letters patent, it cannot build its railway or telephone line. So , we pass the Act in this form, declaring that in that country and subject to the laws of that country, they can build a railway so far as our incorporation of them is concerned-but of course not in Canada or any other British country.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.']

There was a vote of
$2,000,000 last year, and $1,000,000 is asked for this year. I suppose that means that $1,000,000 has been expended. What area of land will be covered by the buildings, what is the locality, and what has been done up to the present time?

This vote of $1,000,000 is required for the purchase of properties, etc., west of the Supreme Court building, namely, the area bounded by Wellington street and the river, as far down as the Perley Home. The block from Bank street to Kent street, down to the river, would afford sufficient space for the new departmental buildings, but in view of the future extension which will be unquestionably required, it would seem to be the part of wisdom to purchase now the whole strip above mentioned as far as the Perley Home. With the existing conservatory and Supreme Court building removed, practically a duplicate of the stately and imposing front of the Parliament Buildings could be secured. A retaining wall or ramp similar to that in front of the Parliament Buildings could be constructed, with a broad flight of steps leading from the level of the lawn to the west of the West Block to the lower level of Bank street. A location would thus be secured for the new departmental buildings which, taken in conjunction with the Parliament grounds, with its natural beauties and advantages, would afford a site of magnificence unsurpassed not only on this continent but throughout the world. The approximate value of the properties is $3,300,000. Deduct expenditure on the above during the fiscal year 1912-13, $882,149.91, also expenditure on the above from 1st April, 1913, to 31st December, 1913, $958,167.59-the two deductions totalling $1,840,917.50-and that gives as the probable amount required to complete the purchase of the properties $1,459,082.50. The appropriation for 1913-14 was $2,000,000, from which deduct the expenditure from 1st April, 1913, to 31st December, 1913, $1,024,430.43, and assumed
expenditure prior to 31st 4 p.m. March, 1914,	$375,569.57-a
total deduction of $1,400,000 -and the revote is therefore $600,000. The new vote applied for in the main Estimates, 1914-15, is $400,000.'
Has the department bought all these lands extending from the Supreme Court building?

All expropriated. The
figures I have given are the estimated cost. I may add that architects are invited to submit sketch designs in a preliminary competition for the erection of departmental and court buildings. From the designs submitted six will be chosen Iby the assessors, the authors of which will be invited to submit more matured designs in a final competition, for which the five unsuccessful competitors will each receive an honorarium of $3,000. Sketch designs are to be in by April 2, 1914. We have selected Mr. Colbutt, of London, England; Mr. Russell, of Winnipeg, the President of the Dominion Association of Architects, and Mr. Mar-chand, a prominent Montreal architect, as judges of the competition.
Will the street that runs parallel to Wellington street ibe closed and occupied by buildings? Whereabouts on the property will the buildings be located?

A landscape gardener has been looking it over for us, and these matters will have to toe settled by a man of that kind. A good deal will depend on the plans submitted under this scheme, and the matter cannot be decided until that point is reached.

How is it that part of the work of expropriation has not yet been completed? I understand that it was the intention from the beginning to buy all this property; part of it has been bought and paid for, but part has not yet been secured by the Government. Is there likely to be any permanent difficulty in securing the rest?

We do not anticipate any permanent difficulty, but, as my hon. friend knows, there are a very large number of property holders in that area. We have appointed valuators and they have made considerable progress in effecting settlements without court proceedings. A few cases, I am afraid, cannot be settled without going to the Exchequer Court. But-before taking these cases to court we are securing as much of the land as we possibly

can, and shou!d any other cases turn up we will take them all to court together.

Is that likely to delay
the project for any considerable time?
No; we have to abide by the price fixed by the Exchequer Court.

Is there no appeal from
the Exchequer Court?
There is an appeal to the Supreme Court.
And to the Privy Council?
Yes, by special leave.

Is it the intention to
gather in the various departmental offices now rented throughout the city and accommodate them in this building?

That is the purpose for
which we are undertaking the work; we want to have all our offices under one roof.

Will sufficient buildings
be erected at first to house all the offices of the Government?
The deputy tells me that the proposed plans will be sufficient to house the offices of the various departments now in all the rented buildings throughout the city.

Will such a building
occupy the whole or only a part of the area purchased?

The plan is that right
below the Supreme Court will be erected a very large office building. Then out on the part overlooking the river will be erected a new Supreme Court building. The place below will be available for additional buildings in the future.

I understand the land
will cost about three millions. Has any conclusion been reached as to what will be expended on the first office building and the Supreme Court building?

The cost of the first two buildings has been roughly extimated at about three million dollars.
Public Buildings, Ottawa-Eastern Block addition, $75,000.
This is to finish the extension of the East Block.

What did that addition
cost?

The chief architect's
estimate at first was $360,000, and we have

spent up to the 31st of March, 1913, $337,617.16. This balance, which is largely for vaults, will complete the work.
Mr. iPARDEE: What Government building is being erected east of the Chateau Laurier?
The examining warehouse.

Have they found a
solid foundation yet?
I am glad to hear for the first time from the architect that they have now got to a solid foundation. It was a tremendous expense.
How much has been expended in getting the foundation?
About half a million dollars. We found >a river down there and some other things, and when we .started we had to go to the bottom.

What did you find
when you got to the bottom?
Rock.	'

Was the work done by
contract?

It was done by day labour at first. We found that with the sort of labour we could secure in Ottawa we were not likely to make headway, and the contract was given to the Foundation Company, Limited, of Montreal.
Is that the same company that operates in New Brunswick?
I do not know. I understand they operate all over the Dominion.
What was the price paid per cubic yard?
It was done on force account.
What percentage of profit did the company receive?
Cost, plus 12i per cent.

I want to warn the minister that if that company is operating in Ottawia as it is operating in New Brunswick, he will want to have not only one inspector but half a dozen inspectors over them, and then the minister will be beaten. They built a bridge over the river St. John at Fredericton, and according to the report just brought down in the Legislature, one pier of that bridge cost between $64,000 and

$65,000. The original pier cost only $8,000 or $9,000. There was something wrong with the foundation, and it went out with the ice last year. This company is a sort of a mystery in our province. The provincial Minister of Public Works does not even know who the directors or officers are; they simply dropped down from heaven, and they gobble up gold by the barrel, and I do not know where they will go with it. They are a most wonderful organization. If they are carrying on the same kind of work on the Ottawa custom house foundation that they are in New Brunswick, my hon. friend had better get back to his former condition, even if it did take two or three inspectors to do the work of one good man who had been dismissed on account of political trouble in the city of Ottawa. My hon. friend the senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) is looking very anxious. It would be very amusing if I were to read to the House some of the correspondence of my hon. friend to the former inspector. I will, however, forego that pleasure just at present unless the minister is very anxious to hear it. The reason why my hon. friend (Mr. Rogers) had to go to this Foundation Company was the interference of my hon. friend the senior member for Ottawa.
No?

The trouble was that mv hon. friend the member for Ottawa wrote to Mr. Inspector: ' Put on this man; he was a good ward worker at the last election. I would like this man appointed to carry water or on some other good easy job. He is not very strong, but he did some work at the last election, and you must find a job for him.' I have seen not one but fifty letters like that from my hon. friend the senior member for Ottawa, written in his own handwriting too. They can be produced if necessary. They are the most remarkable set of documents that I have seen in my lifetime. It is no wonder that my hon. friend the minister says he has had some difldculty in regard to labourers in Ottawa. I remember that one letter was in regard to getting rid of a certain class of European labourers in order to put certain other people in their place. The letters would be very interesting reading to the minister if they were brought ten. his attention. He can have them at any time by asking for them. That is the reason why it became costly to carry on the work as it was being carried on, and that is the reason, I presume, why the minister was compelled to look after this foundation company. He had better look 119
after that company very closely, because, even apart from the friends of my hon. friend the senior member for Ottawa, the work is costing too much.

I appreciate very much
what my hon. friend has stated, and I am free to confess that I think this work has cost a much heavier sum than it should have cost. The Foundation Company have been much slower than we hoped they would be when they first started. I do not know that they have made much greater progress than we were making before we called them in. The work, however, was very difficult, and it was represented that they were experts on this class of work. We were anxious to do the best we could, and that is why the bargain was made with them. I agree, however, with my hon. friend that I would not like to have a similar experience repeated if it could be avoided.

Does it occur to my hon. friend that the practice of letting work on cost plus 12i%, must lend to extravagance, because the contractor does not care a straw how much it costs the Government to carry out the work. He says: The more cost the better; if I can make this work cost $100,000, I shall get $12,500 out of it; if it costs $50,000, I shall get only $6,250. The principle is vicious. A similar case occurred in the city of Fredericton. The contractors had two men carrying water to their workmen from a spring away down the river bank, about half a mile below the work, although the city of Fredericton has as pure water as any city in Canada. The city paid $185,000 or $200,000 to put in a filtration plant a few years ago. The Government, however, was paying the bill, and the contractors wished to find a job for a couple of old men who were not able to do hard work. These men did not go to the spring at all; they went into a house and got their pails filled from the city taps; they had a smoke, and then came back again. That was all right, of course; it gave a job to two men; the country was paying the bill, and the contractors got their 15%. That contract was on the basis of cost plus 15%. The Government was easier then. That is only a small case, but it illustrates the way in which this force account works out. I shall be very much surprised, when the bills are brought in and audited, if the minister will not find hundreds and thousands of dollars worth of work charged for, which will be paid for to this Foundation Com-



pany, just along the line of these two old water carriers in New Brunswick.

While the work has been expensive, I can assure my hon. friend that both myself and the officers of the department have been especially diligent in trying to keep down the expense in every possible way. I do not think there is anything connected with the department regarding which I have taken occasion to call in my officers more regularly and more insistently than I have in respect to this contract, because I felt that it was costing too much. So far as keeping down expense is concerned, I am satisfied that every possible care will be taken by the officers of the department.
How long has this work been in progress ?
A little over a year.

I understand the hon.
minister to say that about half a million dollars have been spent ?
Yes.
No tenders were ever called for this work ?
It was started by day labour and then done on force account.

That is practically day
labour. Force account does not change the system of work in any degree at all. It simply gives to the fortunate man in charge of the work 124% profit, whereas otherwise he would not get as much. I should think that hon. gentlemen sitting behind the minister must feel somewhat aggrieved that this large amount of money is being spent without tenders being called. I [DOT] fancy that we should hear some criticism from our hon. friends opposite. It is unusual for such an enormous amount of money to be spent with so little progress. Is there any information in the department as to the time when this work will be completed ?

The foundation part is
practically completed now.

The Foundation Company
are still on the job, are they not?

Yes, but they are just
finishing up. They have got to the rock during the last few days.

My hon. friend says that they have just got to the rock in the last few days. In what did they start? I was

under the impression that they started in rock.

They started in clay,
quicksand, the river bed, and everything else.

This vast expenditure, made without tender or contract, in contravention of the statute which requires work of this size to be let only by tender and contract, ought to call forth the fullest examination from every member of the committee. The minister should bring down at the earliest possible date the fullest information in regard to the whole matter, showing the amount of money spent previous to the arrangement with the Foundation Company, all other expenditure incurred, whether efforts had been made to come to an arrangement with any ether people than the Foundation Company to complete the work by some other method than by force account, and the contract made with the Foundation Company. All this information should be before the committee before this item is passed. In addition to that, the House should be informed as to whether the Foundation Company have the right to construct the foundation part of the building, or whether their duties under the contract are finished when they find rock bottom. I venture to say that never in the history of this country has there been a case where a government has spent half a million dollars of the people's money in trying to find a foundation on a single building. The whole proceedings in regard to this expenditure ought to be before the House for our supervision before this item is passed.

I think also we are entitled to have information as to the amount of material that has been removed and the different kinds, as this material is usually classified. To be told merely that the work has cost half a million without being told what has been done with the money is rather too meagre information to justify the passing of an item such as this.

If any hon. member has had experience in contracting, he will realize what took place. As I understand it, they started this foundation by day work and worked until they struck quicksand and an underground river. Then experts were called in. Any one who knows anything about contracting would know that a tender could not be expected under these conditions.
Does the hon. gentleman know what occurred in the case of this work?	.
I know a good deal of what occurred. If you will permit me, I will tell.
What responsibility have you in connection with it?

No more than you
have.

We have here the
responsible minister, with the officers of his department, who is supposed to give us the facts.
Have I no right to speak in this House?

If you know more
than the minister does?

Mr. Chairman, I object to being interrupted in this way, especially by a man who ought to know better. He has been in the House long enough to know what courtesies are due amongst hon. members. I am speaking as one who knows something about what a contract in a case like this might have incurred. I know what work like this is, and the hon. members who have been criticising evidently know nothing about it. I am pointing out that under the circumstances of this case no contracting firm would be justified in taking a contract to find a foundation. I presume the expenditure has been large, but at the same time there is no other way; it would be unreasonable to expect these men or any others to make a contract.
Does the hon. gentleman know that the foundation was found there over a year ago?
I do not, neither, I think, does the hon. gentleman.
How did they find that hole to sink so much money in?
Perhaps I may be allowed a word. I think I know as much about this matter as anybody else in this House.
That is right.

I am afraid that some hon. members on the Opposition side are not quite fully acquainted with the circumstances of the case or the extent of this work. This building will extend over a length, I should say roughly, of two 1194
hundred yards. The foundation was started
-and for this I take some responsibility -by day labour, because it was started in the fall, and, in order to give employment to a number of men who were out of work,
I suggested to the former Minister of Public Works, Mr. Monk, that it should be begun by day labour, assuming that it was an ordinary foundation.
When was that?
Nearly two years ago.
In the winter of 1911-12?

went at it in a different way; instead of making holes of ten or twenty feet, as under the old system, they would go down forty or fifty feet, sinking piers and timbers to very great depth, until now, at last, they have found rock at the corner which baffled them. I believe they are down to 130 or 140 feet from the level of the street. So the work has been really of a very unusual character, and I think this expenditure has been fully justified.
Are the foundations in?

The piers are being built up to the level, as I understand it. And, as I have said, the work covers quite an area and a great many holes have to be driven to the rock which is found at different levels. I understand that they have now about completed the work, and the contractor is here ready to go on with the building. With regard to what has been said by the hon. member for Carle-ton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell), of course a great many workmen came to me to get work, and this I tried to get for them. We did not distinguish politically-
Oil, oh.

Now, I tried to treat you fairly-
Mr, FRIPP: There are, of course, special cases. But on the whole it was a good thing for the workingmen of Ottawa and surrounding district-they came here from Hull and many other places. The Foundation Company are doing the work with fewer men but they are high-priced men, expert timbermen, imen who are not afraid to go down a hundred and fifty feet to work with a drill or use any of the appliances they use in order to make sure that they are not in shale but in solid rock. Giving this Company due credit, I think they are expert men. The head of it is a Canadian born who gained his trainng in the United States. He tells me that they have put in foundations all over the United States, carrying on this work as a specialty.

My hon. friend has
given a very interesting description of the difficulties of this work. My hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) stated that none of the hon. members on this side are engineers nor have they had experience and so they do not know anything about it.
I did nut say that.

The hon. gentleman said that we had had no experience and could not realize what had occurred on this work. But we know 'quite well what occurred. When the Government started to construct the foundation of this building, they had in charge a man by the name of Robert Low. Mr. Low was a splendid man-a man who knew his business. He worked at it for some time, and was getting along very well. It is true that the hon. member for Ottawa made a good deal of trouble by asking Mr. Low to find places for thirty or forty men as bookkeepers, timekeepers, water-carriers, and other positions in which they did not have to work, and the thing wias loaded with non-productive employees whose wages the Government had to pay.

Mr. Low was a very good
man, too.

Yes, that is where the
trouble was. Mr. Low was too good a man to do exactly what the hon. member for Ottawa wanted him to do, and after three or four months bickering, the trouble arose. Finally Mr. Low was dismissed; that is one of the things the hon. member for Selkirk did not know anything about, and I am trying to enlighten him. My hon. friend talks about digging a hole 130 feet into the ground as if it were a wonderful engineering feat; he will find hundreds of men throughout Canada who know how to do that. He said the trouble was that the government men were not digging a hole big enough; that they were digging a hole 20 feet in diameter whereas the Foundation Company is digging a hole 40 feet in diameter. It is a wonder they do not dig it 100 feet in diameter, because the bigger the hole the more it costs, and the more commission they get out of it. It takes a wonderful amount of engineering ability to know how to dig a hole twice as big as is necessary. The whole trouble arises from political considerations. If the Government had allowed Mr. Low to go on with the work, there is no question that, with his ability and energy, he would have completed it perhaps a year ago, and it would not have cost the Government half a million dollars either. But Mr. Low had to be dismissed on account of his political opinions, and three men were employed to take his place. As always happens in such cases, these men were not able to do the work, and it was because they blundered about for five or six months that a considerable amount of money was lost. After the incompetent foreman had worked at the job for five or

six months and had lost a lot of money for the Government, the Government were compelled to get somebody who did know how to do the work, and they sent for the Foundation Company. I do not say the Foundation Company did not know how to do the work; I presume they did; but I contend that Mr. Low could have done it just as well. This is but another illustration of the results that are had when the Government allows politics to interfere with proper business methods. The hon. member for Ottawa was not the only man responsible for Mr. Low's dismissal; possibly I owe him an apology for bringing his name into the matter at all. The Conservative members for Nova Scotia are responsible for that-I happen to know something about it, and the minister happens to know something about it, I will say, on behalf of the minister, that it was with very great hesitancy and reluctance that he yielded to the pressure brought to bear upon him. The minister realized that Mr. Low's services were satisfactory, and he did not want to dispense with them. For some time he fought against the demands made by the Conservative members, but finally, when the pressure became sufficiently strong, he had to yield, and Mr. Low was removed from the position. And now my hon. friend is reaping the only result which could be expected from his action in dispensing with the services of a competent man for political purposes. I am glad to know that this carnival of squandering money is about concluded, and that the workmen have found bottom. I do hope the minister will learn a lesson from this matter, and that, especially in the city of Ottawa, he will have the work done not on the per diem basis or by foundation companies on force account, but by calling for tenders. If he does this he will always find some one who has sufficient ability to do such work. It is amusing to hear the hon. member for Selkirk and the hon. member for Ottawa telling us that this was such a peculiar kind of work that no contractors would tender for it.
I said the conditions were peculiar.

It was easy to get men to tender for the foundations of the Quebec bridge, but of course an ordinary contractor has not sufficient ability or knowledge to tender for digging a hole in the earth on Sussex street.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The Canadian Pacific Railway Company had the same foundation
company construct the foundations of t\ Windsor Street station of Montreal, on force account, too.

We will discuss the Canadian Pacific railway when we come to it;
I am speaking now only of this carnival of expenditure that is going on in connection with the work on Sussex street. The hon. member for Selkirk knows better than to say that the Government could not get an engineer or a contractor to estimate on that work. The minister knows that dozens of good contractors in Canada would have been pleased to tender for this work. Perhaps they would not have undertaken to build the foundation for so many thousand dollars, but they would have tendered on schedule rates, and the Government would have paid a certain rate per cubic yard for the removal of the material. The rates would not be very high; they are not removing solid rock there-they are trying to find it, and when they find it they are supposed to stop. There is a suspicion in Ottawa that the Foundation Company do not stop when they get to what ought to be a sufficient foundation; of course, I have no evidence of the truth of that, and I only give it to my hon. friend as a current report. One thing is sure, however, and that is that the Foundation Company did not make any attempt to make the cost any less than it ought to be, and I do not think the hon. member for Ottawa made an honest effort to reduce the cost of the work to any considerable extent. I would like the minister to tell the Committee what percentage of the work was done by days work and what percentage by the Foundation Company.
Did I understand the hon. member for Carleton to say that the foreman who succeeded Mr. Low was incompetent?

I only know that it took three men to do Mr. Low's work. They worked at the job for a few months and had to throw it up; if the hon. gentleman wants any stronger evidence of incompetency, I do not know where we are going to look for it.

Whilst we are discussing Ottawa departmental buildings, I may say that we have not yet reached the item in respect of the particular wmrk which has been discussed this afternoon. The hon. member for Pictou has asked for certain returns in regard to the matter, and I will undertake to see that they are brought

down before we reach that item. We can discuss the matter then, and I will get for my hon. friend the information he asks for with regard to the percentage of the cost.
I would like to have also the total costs up to date.

Did the department make plans and specifications of this work, and generally put themselves in a position to call for tenders?
If they did, what was the estimated cost *of excavation and of the foundation complete. He might also inform us if they had different classifications of expense-so much for removal of clay or rock, and so much for the completed foundation. What was the total estimate of the cost of the foundation and how does it compare with the cost when completed?

All this will be taken
note of and will come down in the form of a return before we reach that item.
Public Buildings, Ottawa-Royal Mint- Refinery-Additional story to building, $35,000.
What is the occasion of this addition to the Mint building?

It is required to give
more room for the work of the Mint. It was asked for by Dr. Bonner on January 15, 1912. In his memorandum he stated that he had been informed by the Dominion Mines Company that they proposed to send all their gold to the Mint, and this, added to the increasing amount received from the Yukon, rendered it necessary to add an upper story to the building, as was, contemplated when the building was erected, so that no structural difficulties will be encountered.
Public Buildings, Ottawa-Victoria Memorial Museum, $40,000.

What is the object of
that vote?
This is a revote of $40,000 asked for the dividing of two large halls into offices, the completing of the auditorium, and electric fixtures. Electric fixtures amount to $20,000.

I hope my hon. friend will not yield to the clamour of certain people for the closing of the museum on Sunday. I think the hon. minister is to be congratulated for having yielded t<y the popular demand in opening that museum on Sunday. I have been there myself on two Sundays, and I can testify to the large fMr. Rogers.]
number of people who visited the various sections. Many people cannot afford the time to visit the museum during the week, and they do so on Sunday, when it is an agreeable recreation for them and very instructive. We surely need not be more pious than they are in England. London is supposed to be a very pious city on Sunday, but, as a matter of fact, all the large museums and even private collections are open on Sunday; and it seems to me that Ottawa, not being more pious than London but equally pious, can afford to open its museum on that day. I hope that my hon. friend, who is also a pious man, will follow his better nature in this case.

There is no intention
whatever of closing the museum on Sunday. I think it is a very desirable thing to have it open so that those who are not able to visit it during the week may do so on that day. I am glad to say that the number visiting the museum is increasing every Sunday and is evidence of the fact that the opening of the museum is appreciated by the public.

Any one who looks
at the Estimates and the money we vote for Ottawa every year must be struck by the existing situation. Last year we voted and expended $3,185,000. This year we are expending $2,000,000. In view of the tremendous expenditures that have been made aind must necessarily be made in the future, the time has surely arrived when Parliament should deal with the position of Ottawa in relation to the whole Confederation and put her in the same position that Washington is in the States. The manner in which municipal affairs have been handled in this city, the position in regard to the water question, visitors for the past four years having been unable to drink the water provided by the civic authorities, and various other incidents, together with this vast expenditure, create a situation in which the Government of the day should seriously consider taking up the whole question and dealing with it properly. I find that in Ottawa the public opinion is daily growing that we ought to have the commission system of government, and I believe it would be in the interest of the whole country if Canada would take pride in her national capital and create a non-partisan commission who would administer the affairs of this city. As it is, we have such discussions as that which has just taken place, showing, right under the nose of Parliament, the nauseat-

ing effect of patronage in every one of these expenditures of a public and national character. How long is this present anomalous situation to continue? It was all very well in the earlier stages of Confederation; but any one with any pride in his country must realize that it is our duty to provide for the future, and here in our capital city we should provide for a system of government that would guarantee to every citizen of Canada who came here, and to every citizen of any other country who visited our national capital, such a condition of affairs in relation to municipal government and all other things as would make us proud of our capital city. That is not the situation to-day. I would press upon the minister and the Government generally the wisdom and importance, in the interest not alone of Ottawa, but of the whole of Canada, of seriously grappling with this question at an early day.

There are two
sides to the question raised' by my hon. friend. Municipal government is claiming more and more attention in the great country to the south of us. I wish my hon. friend had the felicity, as I had, of listening to the City Chamberlain of New York last Saturday, in an address before the Canadian Club. He would there have learned from a very clean-cut and brilliant intellect, one of many that are growing up among the young men of the United States, that municipal government is cMming more and more attention from the rising generation there. My hon. friend seems to have vast confidence in the federal Government in the abstract.
I was not suggesting that the Government should control the city, but that a commission might be created such as exists in other capitals.

I was going to say my hon. friend seems to have vast confidence in the federal Government in the abstract, but very little confidence in the concrete. Perhaps I misunderstood my hon. friend. But he did say that he wanted to see reproduced in this country what exists at Washington, D.C. The gentleman to whom I referred a moment ago said on Saturday that he would be very glad if any Canadian who was enamoured of the particular form of municipal government they have at Washington, D.C., and anxious to introduce it in Ottawa, would first visit Washington to acquaint himself with the
criticisms that are being passed upon the methods of administration of the federal district of that capital. I do not know much about the question myself, but I thought it right to introduce at this time the most recent information the people of Ottawa have had the chance of hearing from one who is sufficient of an expert to have obtained the very important position of city chamberlain of New York.

The question before the House has broadened somewhat, and I would like to see it approached in a broad way, even so far as to review the suitability of the present location of the capital of Canada. In Australia they are starting de novo. They have found the best possible location for the capital, climatically and from a sanitary point of view, and have begun a splendid system of capital planning. In doing that, they hope to have a model city.
Would you call the new capital Carberra?

I do not know what 1 would call it; that is what they call the new capital of Australia. What I wish to discuss is whether the selection of more [DOT]than 50 years ago of Bytown, of the city of Ottawa, is the best possible location for our capital to-day? Are not the climatic conditions here of the most rigorous kind?
You should come to Vancouver.
Some people think a better climate would be found in the West. It might be found on the coast, or on lake Erie or lake Ontario.
You are thinking of Toronto.

If you ask me, I would say on the bay of Quinte, between Montreal and Toronto, and on the line of the great Transcontinental railway going by Quebec, Montreal, Toronto, Sudbury, Port Arthur and Winnipeg. Ottawa is off that road. Perhaps some day we may have to review this question, and if it is to be reviewed it might be a good investment to acquire a large area of land to be devoted to the use of a great national capital for Canada. Let us take the case of Ottawa. It has a rigorous climate, and in summer it is not an attractive city.
Oh, oh.

Anyway, hon. gentlemen are all most anxious to get 5 p.m. away from this city in June. It is an impossible summer capital -I will put it that way-and all our legislation is coonskin-coat legislation. Everybody has to wear a coonskin coat, or should wear one, and I do not think Canadians are at their best, for the purposes of legislation, in a climate so rigourous as this happens to be. With conditions as they are in this city-and the hon. member for Pictou just now said that those who have been here for years cannot even get pure water to drink-it might be well worth while for Parliament to review the whole situation. As to the possibilities of life and improvement on this continent, and we are just beginning to find ourselves. While I would not say a word as to the wisdom of the Royal lady who made the choice of Ottawa as a capital, I do say that it does not quite meet the requirements of Canada to-day.
Would the hon. member say in what division of Toronto he would like to have the capital ?
I am not saying that at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid the discussion is drifting from the item.
Possibly it is within the purview of discussion of this item.
Has Parliament the power to change the capital ?
It can do anything it wants to do.
No, it cannot.
I [DOT] am sorry to hear a member say that it cannot.
You would like to have it in Toronto ?
Toronto is not a bad city; it has a good public opinion.
That depends on the point of view.

Perhaps Hamilton might be a good place for the capital. But this question is coming up both in the East and the West. I say we have not the best possible capital to-day. If the whole matter is to be reviewed eventually, it may be unwise to embark on expenditures involving hundreds of millions of dollars.
Not so much as that.

I do not know what they will be eventually. We have not committed ourselves to much so far, comparatively speaking. If Parliament is to sit all the year round-and that seems to be coming-we ought to have a capital that is fairly possible in summer and winter, and our present capital is not in either.

In this 20th century, to talk of removing the Capital of Canada is, in my humble judgment, an absurdity. Many of us, no doubt, like the hon. gentleman for South York, would like our own city to be the capital.
'Mr. W. F. MACLEAN:	Please do not
impute to me something I did not say.

I am not sas'ing Ottawa is the best place in Canada in which to live, but I do say that a city in which has been spent millions of dollars in the erection of public buildings, and which has within its limits thousands of civil servants who have made homes here for themselves, and in which many millions of dollars have been spent in beautifying it, will remain, notwithstanding the arguments of my hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean), the capital city of Canada. The hon. gentleman said that Canadians were not at their best in coon-skin coats. I do not know about that. Canadians are a hardy race, and they rather like the long winter months. Those of us who are obliged to stay in Ottawa all the time, during the session, and to attend to our parliamentary duties all the time, coming as we do from the far East and the far West, would perhaps have more reason for wanting the capital city changed than my hon. friend from South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean). At all events, it is simply absurd, in this year of grace, to ask that the capital of Canada should be removed from Ottawa.

Of course, if there ever should be any serious thought of moving the capital from Ottawa, I would suggest that possibly the city of Kingston would be an ideal spot. However, it is my view that not in the whole Dominion of Canada, from ocean to ocean, all things considered, can there be found a place more suitable for the capital of our Dominion than right here. Any person, with an artistic eye, who walks out on the hill behind these buildings, will view a panorama of natural beauty that cannot be excelled in America; I doubt if it can be excelled anywhere on the continent of Europe. I am not in accord with the idea of moving the capital from its

present location. The remarks which have fallen from the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) in regard to the climatic disabilities of Ottawa, will probably give us some tangible idea as to why we have seen so very little of that hon. gentleman at the Capital during the sessions of Parliament. I would remind him of a remark made by a former Governor General of Canada, to the effect that possibly Canada's cold climate was Canada's warmest friend. I care not whether the members of Parliament have to come here in coon-skin coats or in silk hats, they can very well stand the climate of Ottawa for the few months of the parliamentary session. I repeat that, all things considered, Ottawa is the best possible location we could get for the capital city of our Dominion. It is right on the line between the great province of Ontario and the great province of Quebec, which are the very basis of our country, and it is possibly not far from the present centre of population of the Dominion. The Government is justified in spending money in Ottawa, in the view that it shall always remain our capital. As to the formation of a federal district, that is a matter which should receive the most careful consideration from the Government, before any step is taken in that direction.
Has any provision been made in the new buildings for accommodating the Royal Society of Canada, as promised by the Minister of Public Works?

I do not know that I
made any promise. When the deputation waited on me, these Estimates had already been brought down'.
Will the hon. gentleman make a promise for the future?
Can the minister give any assurance' that the foundation of the Royal Victoria Museum building is now secure?

There is a difficulty in
connection with the tower of the Museum, which has separated to some extent from the main building. It is not regarded by the architect as being very serious, but it is sufficiently serious to require attention. The purpose is to attend to it in the very near future.

Is it the opinion of the architect that the settling of the foundation has now ceased, or is the opening around the ceiling of the building likely to become greater as time goes on? It is in
a very unsightly condition and should be attended to.

The architect informs me that he is now discussing a proposition with a view to strengthening the foundation. I do not think he is very clear on whether there is going to be any greater separation of the tower from the main building, but we will have the matter very carefully looked into.
In reference to the discussion about moving the capital city of Canada to some other locality, of course, if anything like that were ever contemplated, it would be my duty to put in a word for the city of Winnipeg, which is the centre of the Dominion, and one of the growing cities of our country.
It is colder than here.

That may be, but it has many other advantages which make one . forget the coldness of its climate. We have anticipated the idea of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) to some extent. He will quite agree that it would be impossible to give any intelligent consideration to a suggestion regarding a federal city without first having certain necessary information.
I quite agree that there are two sides t< the question. Many people are in favour of the idea of a federal city similar to that of Washington, and many people, for various reasons, oppose such an undertaking on the part of the Government. In order that we may have an intelligent understanding of the idea, the Government has gone the length of appointing a commission to prepare a plan. This step has been taken by the Government, without in any way committing itself to the idea of a federal city, in view of the expressed wishes of a great many people who believe in this proposal. That commission consists of Mr. H. F. Holt and Sir Alexander Lacoste, of Montreal, Mr. Frank Darling and Mr. Home Smith, of Toronto, the mayor of the city of Ottawa and the mayor of the city of Hull, whoever they may be, during their respective terms of office. Perhaps by the next session of Parliament they will have reduced their ideas to a plan that will enable us to give at least intelligent consideration to the proposal, and to express our views either for or against it.
Will that plan include the acquiring of a large area of territory?

It includes the planning of the capital. There are several ideas

that necessitate consideration in this respect. With all due respect to the civic government of Ottawa, if there is one consideration more than another tnat would prompt me at all events to support a proposal for the removal of the capital from this city, it is the manner in which the municipal organization of the city of Ottawa, not this year alone, hut every year, have treated us in respect to the supplying of pure water for the people who come to this city from time to time. In my humble judgment this is a very dangerous condition of affairs, and it is to be regretted, because this Parliament, as has been said, has spent a great deal of money in attempting to beautify this city. In return for that, we naturally think that the residents of Ottawa, through their municipal Government, should at least undertake to supply us with pure water and make us feel that we are not taking any risks in drinking the water given to us from day to day. I have only mentioned this matter of town planning in order that my hon. friend may see that we are not overlooking the importance of his suggestion, and that we have gone that far in order that at a future date we may be ab'e to give careful attention to that suggestion.

Has my hon. friend not been rather severe in his strictures upon the city of Ottawa in regard to not supplying Parliament with pure water, for the reason that it is only in very recent times that Parliament has taken to drinking water?

I think I can safely say that the people of the city of Ottawa will thank the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) for bringing this matter to the attention of Parliament. A short time ago a vote was submitted to the people of Ottawa as to whether or not they would desire the Government to form Ottawa into a federal district, and it was carried by a very large majority. Personally I wish to place myself on record as being in favour of that idea. My short experience as a representative of the people of Ottawa in this House, and my connection with the municipal government, have led me to the conclusion that it is absolutely necessary in the best interest of the city that some such scheme as that shall be considered and carried into effect.
With regard to the water question, I think that the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) must take some blame to himself as a member of the present Gov-
ernment. I wish to point out that the trouble in regard to the supply of water by the municipality, for use in the buildings here and for the people of Ottawa, has arisen within a very few years from a cause which was preventable. Hon. gentlemen in this House seem to forget that. The fault did not lie so much in the supply itself as it lay with this Parliament in allowing municipalities to dump their sewage into the Ottawa river above the present limits of the city of Ottawa. That is the cause of the trouble, together with some negligence on the part of civic officials which was the immediate cause of the last typhoid epidemic. The Government of the day is so vitally interested in the city of Ottawa that I am of the opinion that, unless it acts in a paramount way and compels the municipality to take water from a proper source, we shall have a continuation of this trouble. Surely this Government, which is willing to contribute such a large sum of money for the bringing of pure water to the city of Ottawa, is as much interested in the matter as are the people of Ottawa. I suggest that the hon. Minister of Public Works should not find fault with the municipal government of the city, but rather that he and the Government behind him have the power to say to the city of Ottawa: We are as much interested financially as you are. We have invested in Ottawa as much if not more money than the people of this city; we will investigate the water supply, and we will say how much we are willing to contribute to a supply, if it is a proper one. In the city of Ottawa to-day are two factions fighting over where the supply of water shall come from. It devolves on the Government to say: We will only support that scheme which we think, after proper investigation, independent as we are, is the proper source from which to get a full and pure supply of water for the residents of Ottawa and the people who come here from time to time. I think that is the duty resting upon the Government. If the Government take such a stand as that, they will settle this question once and for all.
In conclusion, I desire to say that the form of municipal government here is neither better nor worse than that in any other city having the same system. With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), I also had the pleasure of listening to the lecture by the City Chamberlain of New York, and he did not impress me so strongly as he impressed the hon. gentleman. I believe that a federal district is the system which

should be adopted for the city of Ottawa, because we are peculiarly situated here, interlocked as we are with the Government of the day in the management of the affairs of the capital city of the Dominion. I implore the Government to take a decided stand on the question of what shall be the proper source of water supply for the city of Ottawa. I believe that is the only way in which the question will be settled, and it will take some years to bring it to a final and proper conclusion.

I would be very sorry indeed if the Government saw fit to follow the advice of my hon. friend. I am sorry also to see introduced into discussion in this House the question as to what any man may consider the proper settlement of this unfortunate dispute in Ottawa. It is not very hard to see, from the remarks of my hon. friend from Ottawa, which scheme he wishes adopted; but, I am not going to refer to that at all. I know of no hon. member who has suffered more through Ottawa water than I have, and I speak with some feeling. I am just as anxious as any other man for a pure supply of water for the city of Ottawa. I do not think, however, that the Government has the right to say: We will contribute if the municipal authorities decide the question one way, and we will not contribute if they decide it another way. There is too big a question of principle involved, because the very moment the Government take that stand, they have to go to the further extent of saying:	We are going to control the
municipal authorities of the city of Ottawa; for the very reason that, when they take that stand, they are controlling the municipal authorities.
I am sufficiently a home-ruler to believe that the people of Ottawa are the ones to settle this question. They will get through playing the game of politics after a little while-for that is all it has amounted to for the last two or three years. No one can read the Ottawa newspapers and spend isix months or more of the year in Ottawa as we do without seeing what the game is-purely a political game being worked by the municipal politicians in Ottawa, many of them, I believe, having an eye on higher realms of politics. The people will get tired of it. There is enough common sense, sound judgment and business ability in the electorate of Ottawa-the men who have an interest in the city greater than we have, the men who p.ay the taxes and must continue to pay the taxes-to reach a solution
of this difficulty. I have great faith in the people. I have found that after they get through with their political schemes the common sense of the people comes to the front and decides on the course that on the whole is the best. I believe we haye a pretty good system of municipal government all over Canada. We make our mistakes, but in the end things work out for the public benefit. I hope that the Government instead of following the advice of tne hon. member for Ottawa (Mir. Fripp) will simply say to the people:	Go ahead and
do what is best. I think they will decide for the best, and then I hope the Government will give them assistance to work out the plans with success. I believe the Government should contribute very largely to the water supply of the city of Ottawa, for, as the Minister of Public Works has said, we have to come here and we and our families are dependent to some extent on what the Ottawa authorities do for us. Therefore, we are vitally interested in having a pure wiater supply. But I do not think this Government has any right to step in and say to the people, you must do this or we will not contribute.

I think this has been a valuable discussion. It has brought out the fact that Parliament has within its purview the question of capital-planning, and that is a big undertaking. It has brought out the fact that this Government has in its purview the development of the city here from a municipal point of view and has also the expense of a great deal of money on public buildings. It has also brought within the discussion the question of the government of this city. These are all very important questions, involving great sums of money and the comfort of great numbers of people. And the city of Ottawa has its responsibility in this situation. And it is not a bad idea if the citizens of Ottawa are given to understand' that much depends on them and they cannot throw their burdens altogether on Parliament; and it may be necessary for the Government to consider the question even of location of the capital. It is mainly from that point of view that I approached it this afternoon. I think it is a good idea that Ottawa people should be given to understand that they have duties in this matter. They are going to vote at au early date on. the water question, about which we hear so much in Parliament and read so much in the press. The citizens of Ottawa, if well advised, will show that they

have municipal spirit, that they are prepared to assume their responsibilities. It is' well that they should understand that we are watching their conduct and policy, and that it has not been up to the present time very satisfactory to the Parliament of Canada and to the people who have to come here in connection with Parliament.

I would like to say just a word in conclusion. The idea of a federal district in which Canada's capital should be is one that has long been viewed with favour by many people in this country. The citizens of Ottawa, those immediately connected with the Government of the country by employment in the Civil Service or dependent on them in a greater or lesser degree, are not an industrial people and conditions in Ottawa are such that in a great many respects the city occupies a position exactly like that of Washington in the United States. Indeed, the eloquent gentleman who leads the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has repeatedly spoken of Ottawa as ' the Washington of the North,' and in a most distinctive sense that language is absolutely true. That the idea is one which has been found worthy the consideration of the Government, I think is a matter of congratulation. This is not a political question in any sense. Of course, if we take into consideration the situation in Washington, we find a district, a seat of government peopled, as is Ottawa, very largely by those connected with the Government in greater or lesser degree. But there is no representation of those people in congress. That I regard as the necessary consequence of the establishment of such a district. I have sat in close proximity to my genial friend from Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) in this House, and I am bound to say that no other hon. member need envy the representative of a city like Ottawa. Both he and his hon. colleague all through this Parliament have been deluged by a flood of people who wish to serve their country for a consideration, to a greater degree than one could imagine, to a degree which must impair the usefulness of one who represents such a constituency. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark), who indulged in some caustic comment on the idea that I should have suggested anything in the House that in some way was to the interest of the Government, perhaps has not familiarized himself sufficiently with the conditions that exist on this side of the
Atlantic in relation to this or other matters to warrant him in speaking as an authority.
I said I was not an authority; I quoted an authority.

My hon. friend ventured to quote a gentleman who came here to speak but who, a f-iend from Ottawa tells me-I did not attend the Canadian Club meeting myself-delivered a lecture which did not appeal to him. If my hon. friend had not been carried away by the eloquence of that gentleman, he would probably have discovered that Mr. Bruere is a very tyro in municipal legislation, so much so that his selection by Mayor Mitchell was a great surprise to the people of New York because of Mr. Bruere's lack of experience in regard to civic matters. I do not think that any hon. gentleman in this House should declare ex cathedra that the people of this country or the men of this Parliament must accept Mr. Bruere's views as the last word in municipal government. As one who has visited Washington and seen the methods of government there, I think that every one will agree that the federal district in the case of Washington has been a success. With all deference to Mr. Bruere and his advocacy of ideal municipal systems, whether here or in the United States, the commonly accepted view of men who represent the whole of the United States and who are interested in Washington, as well as that of the civil servants who happen to be there, is that Washington is a creditable capital of their great republic. The public buildings, the care of the streets, the management of public utilities and services that enter into municipal life, are all on a par with the best to be found elsewhere. Every visitor who has gone there will agree with that statement, I am glad that the Government has moved in this matter. I think that the whole of Canada from one end to the other is as much interested in this capital of our nation as the man who resides here. Its permanence, it beauty, its representative character for the whole country, are matters that I say, as a Nova Scotian, I am as much interested in as the man who happens to live here, and matters to which the Government of this country should give particular attention.
I have always been of opinion that the federal district should be reproduced in Canada.
What did this commission cost? Being a farmer, I want to know what things cost.

The commission is purely an honorary one, consisting of six members, of whom two are the mayors of the cities of Ottawa and Hull. Half the expenses are to be borne by those cities and half by the Government. No definite estimate ha^s yet been made as to the total cost, but it will probably amount to $20,000 or $25,000.

I do not pretend to be an authority on the subject which has been discussed this afternoon by the hon. member for Pictou, but it seems to me that in the very fact of extending the jurisdiction of the commission to the province of Quebec, beyond the limits of Ottawa, there is an argument in favour of the establishing of a federal district. I am not committed to one idea more than another, but I would point out that the spending of large sums of money in the capital of the Dominion will excite the jealousy of other municipal governments, unless you make Ottawa a federal district. After all, the city of Ottawa obtains the benefit, to a certain extent, of any improvements which are made, because of the consequent increase in the value of property. I think that public opinion in Ottawa, generally speaking, favours the idea of a federal district. I do not say that it is the best system, but if you extend the powers of the commission beyond the city of Ottawa, including Borden City and Britannia, for instance, you immediately bring the attention of the public to the fact that there is a certain district around the Government buildings which is under the immediate surveillance and control of the federal authorities. For my own part, I think it is worth while studying this question. Canada is a growing country, and in some respects I do not object to imitating the course taken by the United States. I have never heard any criticism, except that which was made this afternoon, against the federal district idea at Washington. Of course, there may be some difliculties connected with its administration, but any one who has occasionally been at Washington and has had a superficial view of the city, must admit that it is indeed a great capital, and that the monuments there are a credit to the United States republic. During our tenure of office, when we started to beautify the city of Ottawa by the appointment of a commission who were given a large amount to spend every year, quite a good deal of criticism was made by persons in other parts of the country. The people said: Why do you
spend so much money on improvements in Ottawa ? We said: It is for the capital of your country. But they said: that increases the value of the municipality of Ottawa, gives additional value to city property, and we do not see why Quebec, Toronto, Montreal, Halifax and the other large cities should not get their share of that money. This is a popular argument, and one which has some logic in it. I do not object to any expenditure for the purpose of beautifying the capital of the Dominion. I do not share the view of the hon. member for South York that we should consider the idea of changing the capital. Of course, the city of Montreal was the one'which should have been the capital of Canada foT all time, but the Tories prevented that in 1849. I quite admit that there is no place in Canada like Ottawa for the capital of the Dominion. I would call the attention of the minister to the fact that he has not answered my 'question with regard to space in the new buildings for the Royal Society. I hope to commit him to the providing of a building of sufficient accommodation for that society.

I am afraid my hon. friend will have to wait for a definite answer until the Supplementary Estimates are brought down.
