M:r. BOULAY: Mr. Chairman, may I be allowed by the committee to add a few words to the remarks that have just been made in reference to the city of Ottawa? I fully concur in the remarks of my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) as to Ottawa having been selected as the capital. The matter was fully considered when the fathers of the Confederation selected Ottawa to he the capital, and I do not feel inclined, as the iron, member for South York, to criticise their action.
Now, with regard to the question of forming Ottawa into a federal district, as was suggested by several hon. members this afternoon, I do not countenance this idea, because I have already strongly criticised that suggestion the very first time I 'heard of it. Ottawa has the benefit of a yearly subsidy amounting to $60,000, during twenty years, for the improvement of her streets and squares. This city is the seat of Government, and as such, gets the greater part of public moneys on account of the fact that it is here that we find the largest number of high-salaried public servants.

Therefore, I believe that the city of Ottawa is in a 'better position than any other city to provide for its own municipal requirements. We have a great number of other cities whicfh are not so favoured and are obliged to bear heavy taxation for the maintenance of their streets and parks, without asking for any assistance from the Government. For my part, even if I should be the only one to object to this change, I would surely never favour such a measure.
On the 18th instant, when the Estimates of the Secretary of State were before the committee, I made some remarks about the employees of the Archives and the Victoria Museum and the minister replied to me that these men were not under his control. I would like to know from the Minister of Public Works if these men are under the Department of Public Works.

The firemen, engineers
and elevator men come under the Public Works Department, but that is all.
Those in whom I am interested were receiving the visitors. I am anxious to know from which department they come.

Apparently they are not
under this department, but I shall let the hon. member know after dinner.
Public Buildings, Toronto-New Dominion buildings, $500,000.
What is the reason for this building?

It is a new post office
for Toronto.

We hear a lot of talk
about a federal square in Toronto. Is the minister carrying out that idea?
No, we are not carrying out that idea at all.
Is the new post office on the same site as the old one?
Yes.
Is it an addition to the old one?

It will be a new building entirely.
Public Buildings, Nova .Scotia-Amherst_
New post office, inclusive of 6 per cent interest on balance due on site, $30,000.

When was this site
bought?

The site has not been
purchased, it was expected when the estimate was put in that we would have had

it expropriated and this is merely an estimate.
Amherst drill hall, $70,000.

How large a place is
Amherst?
Between 10,000 and 12,000.

Will $70,000 finish the
drill hall? I see that $30,000 was voted last year of which there is a revote of $10,000. That would be $20,000 expended, making with this $90,000 for a place of 10,000 or 12,000. Will this $70,000 complete the work?

I do not believe it will
finish it, it will cost about $115,000 all told.

I may as well say now
as at any other time that I am perfectly in accord with the erection of public buildings in reason, but I think it is ridiculous, in a place of 10,000 or 12,000, to spend $115,000 for a drill hall.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I think it includes
an armoury.

Even so. Fifty or sixty
thousand dollars for a building for 10,000 or 12,000 inhabitants is absolutely enough, and I think that is the opinion of the people of this country. There is reason in all things, but no possible reason, in a country like ours-for we are not a military country in any sense-to build an armoury and drill hall in a town of 10,000 or 12,000 to cost $120,000.

I endorse the
opinion expressed by my hon. friend from Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). I speak not so much my own individual opinion, because I am afraid I might be suspected, as I am well known to have views a little different from the ordinary inhabitants of even Canada on the general question of armaments; but I would like to endorse my hon. friend's view that there is a strong feeling in the country on this subject. I hear it expressed, irrespective of politics, by different men. I have received representations in writing on the subject, that we have been spending too much money on this particular line of outlay. I am not speaking from a party standpoint. If I were speaking as a party man, I would take my seat and let this expenditure go on. I speak as a patriotic citizen of the country, and I express the opinion coming to me from many men, irrespective of party.

I also wish to say a few words along the same line. I asked for a

return as to the number of drill halls built since 1911 and the number promised or under construction since that time. I figured out that the total number that had been built went up in cost somewhere in the neighbourhood of $492,000, and there had been promised drill halls to about the same expense to be built in the future. I quite agree in this matter, if it is done in reason, there is no harm; but an expenditure since 1911 of $1,000,000 on drill halls in this country is going too far altogether. There is no question that to a certain extent military matters must be carried on in this country, but we should not go to such extremes as this in the erection of drill halls and armouries. In many small towns particularly, where there are small regiments, they have become practically nothing more or less than clubs, at which men associate, with very little reference to military matters.
And I wish to enter my protest, not in a partisan or any narrow way, but most emphatically, against expenditures of this kind running into the amount of money that drill halls have run into. I never did approve of drill halls to any large extent. In the large centres they are very good things if an appropriate amount of money is spent according to the size of the town; but to build drill halls promiscuously, and to go on increasing our military expenditure, as we have done from year to year does not seem to me to be in keeping with the spirit of Canada; and I do not believe that either on this side of the House or on the other will such expenditures be fully endorsed. Perhaps the Government has been carried away in this matter. At any Tate, I think a very careful consideration of expenditures of that kind is certainly in order at the present time.

When a drill hall is
built in a city like Amherst, is the site given by the municipality, or does the department purchase it?
In many cases the sites have been given.
What did this particular one cost?

It was transferred by the Militia Department to the Public Works Department after the building was partly under way. We have not the information as to whether the site was given, or was paid for by the department.
Would the minister get that- information?

Certainly.

The House in Committee on Bill No. 74, respecting the Central Ontario Railway.- Mr G. V. White. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

Who is the father of
this Bill?

The Bill is in the
name of Mr. White, of Renfrew. It provides for an extension of time, and the committee passed the Bill exactly as applied for. The draftsmen of this Bill did something that I feel like commending them for: They described the location so that the renewal told exactly where the line is to run, thus rendering it unnecessary to refer to the former statute. We checked that [DOT]over to see that the printing was the same, and it was. We granted an extension of time, because some of the work had been [DOT]done and some money expended. We have recast section 3 of the Bill as printed, because it is not the language which we generally use, and we have made it what we may call our model clause-that the company may commence to construct their unconstructed portion, because they have constructed some portions of the railway, and they have not yet commenced certain other portions of it as originally described.
What part of the road has been constructed?

I have not a note
in my minute book as to the exact portion ; simply the note that this section must be amended because part of the railway has been constructed.
Is this the railway company which claims certain land subsidies from the province of Ontario?
No. The company to which my hon. friend refers is one that we have dealt with earlier in the session, namely, the Central Railway Company ef Canada.

It is about the same
name.

This is the Central
Ontario Railway and the other is the Central Railway Company of Canada.
Is my hon. friend satisfied from what he has heard in the committee that this charter ought to be given?

Yes, we thought that it was a bona fide matter.
On section 3-limitation:

Do I understand that
the limitation is less than in the original Bill?

No, we gave them the usual time-two years to commence, five years to complete.

During the last four

the Barcelona Traction, Light and Power Company, Limited, the Brazilian Traction, Light and Power Company, Limited, and the British America Nickel Corporation, Limited, which were passed last year and are being amended. This is a case where a company has letters patent in Canada. It wants to go into a foreign country to build a railway and telephone line, and to use its Canadian incorporated name. When it gets to that foreign country, it is told that, on those letters patent, it cannot build its railway or telephone line. So , we pass the Act in this form, declaring that in that country and subject to the laws of that country, they can build a railway so far as our incorporation of them is concerned-but of course not in Canada or any other British country.

Bear River public building, $4,000.

['This is a vote of $3,000, for a tower clock; $2,000 and $1,000 for sidewalks in connection with municipal undertakings around the building.

Is that Bear River, in Digby county?
Yes.
What is the population of Bear River?
It is estimated at 1,500.
It is not necessary to estimate it when reference can be made to the census returns. Does it appear in the census returns at all?
This is simply a revote; the matter has not been taken up at all.

This amount is in the Estimates, and I presume it is intended to spend the money. If the minister has not the information, surely the officials of his department can tell him what the population of Bear River is.

The post office inspector reported on February 26, 1912, that the population of the town is 1,500, and is
steadily growing. Bear River is situated on a navigable river which enters the Annapolis basin and connects with the bay of Fundy. In former days shipbuilding was carried on extensively at Bear River. It is an important port of entry; sea-borne freights come freely to 'its waters. It is situated some five miles up the river from Bear River railway station, where it makes connection with the Dominion Atlantic railway. The 'townsite is a most picturesque one; Bear River is widely known as one of the greatest beauty spots in Nova Scotia.

I venture to say that the population of Bear River is not one-quarter of 1,500; I suppose that amount includes 'the population of the whole polling subdivision of Bear River. Bear River is a Ismail village in the county of Digby, and T fancy that the population of the village itself is not more than 400. In the past protests have been made against the expenditure of money for erecting public buildings in towns very much larger than Bear River. Our friends on the other side sit behind the minister quite complacently when he asks the committee to vote $4,000 for the erection of a public building in a village the size of Bear River.
Is the money likely to be spent this year?
I am not in a position to give my hon. friend a definite answer; I do not really know why the money was not spent last year.
Has a site been purchased?
No.
For what purpose is the building to be erected?
It is to be used as a post office.
What is the revenue of the post office at the present time?

What is the salary of the
postmaster?
Is it the policy of the minister to erect public buildings
in every place in the country where there is a post office having a similar revenue?
It certainly is not.

Why has the minister
selected Bear River as a place in which to spend $4,000 on a public building, excluding all the other villages of at least the same size?

I can give my hon.
friend no special reason. I found the vote here when I took charge of the department, and it appears to be still here, unexpended.

It seems strange that the hon. minister should keep this amount in the Estimates year after year merely to deceive the people of that village and to give them the impression that they are going to have a public building. Personally, I have no objection to the erection of a public building at Bear River; it is one of the prettiest little villages in the Annapolis valley. But the minister does not even know whether or not the land has been purchased or a site arranged for.
No land has been purchased.
That is worse still.

The policy of erecting buildings of this kind instead of paying rentals is surely a good one. The rental of a post office having a revenue of $1,976 would necessarily be $250 a year. The point that some hon. gentlemen are trying to make is that the Government should not erect this building. I say they should, and that they should erect similar buildings wherever they can.
What rental is the Government now paying for the post office?

I do not think we are
paying any rent.

In Nova Scotia no rentals
are paid for post offices in villages the size of Bear River, so the erection of a public building there would effect no saving whatever. I find that Bear River does not appear at all in the census returns for 1911. I thjnk this item ought to be allowed to stand until we get further information with regard to it.

In reference to the remarks of the hon. member for West Peterborough, I may say that I plainly stated that I had no objection whatever to the erection of a public building at Bear River. I do not

wish the hon. gentleman to misconstrue my remarks and to charge me with something of which I am not guilty. What I object to is the Government putting this amount in the Estimates year after year and not spending the money.

What is the
estimated cost of this building?
We have not made an estimate yet.

What is the information on
which the $4,000 vote was passed last year?

The information in the report of the post office inspector is that the town does a large business and has a large tourist trade, and it is necessary at certain times of the year to give special accommodation to that trade. The population -was estimated, in a report of September 8 last, at 1,500. There is a grist mill, granite works, a threshing mill, a carriage factory, two hotels and 250 houses. The number of boxes in the local post office is 216 of which 168 are rented, so it cannot be a very small place if that is the condition. The population of the town is likely to increase according to the report. A pulp mill and paper mill are likely to be established, which will still further increase the population. The inspector recommends that if a post office building is erected in this town it should be 30 feet by 40 feet.
Has the minister any information as to the amount of customs duties collected there?

The customs duties
amounted to $1,739.81. The money orders issued were $19,394 and the money orders paid $18,901.

It does appear as though
the minister has not the information one would expect if he seriously intended to erect this building. He has no estimate as to the cost Of the building and it seems to me that if it is intended to erect it it ought to be erected. If he is not going to erect it it ought to be struck out of the Estimates. There is not much to be gained by voting the money unless it is to be expended except as an inducement to every other village in Canada to ask for a building.

I do not think the
hon. gentleman can be serious in stating that he estimates the population of this village at about one-quarter of fifteen hundred. I was there last summer and I would estimate the population at at least

one thousand. That estimate is home out by the information given by the minister in regard to the number of houses and the number of boxes in the post office. It is not unfair to estimate five people to a house, and that would place the population at twelve hundred and fifty. It is not unfair to make an estimate in the same way as to the number of boxes. There are 168 boxes, and many who have not boxes, so I think that an estimate of three hundred or four hundred is decidedly under the mark.

I do not object to Bear River having a public building. I believe it is entitled to one and personally I would like to see every village in Nova Scotia with a population of fifteen hundred have a public building. My friends, I think, are rather kicking that the building is not going to be built as quickly as they would like. I wish to bring to the attention of the minster several places in South Cape Breton which I think are entitled to public buildings. We have some of the largest towns in Nova Scotia in that riding. Sydney and Glace Bay are both equipped with fairly good public buildings. But there i3 the town of New Waterford, an incorporated town of probably six thousand or seven thousand which has sprung up in the last five years. The population has increased to between six thousand and seven thousand in the last two years. Our post office there is a disgrace to modern civilization, especially in a, town of that size. My friend the Minister of Customs last year announced his attention to establish ia customs outport there, from Glace Bay or Sydney. Would the minister have his inspector of public buildings this summer look over that situation? I think that he will give the minister sufficient data to encourage him to provide for the erection of a public building there. Then we have the village of Reserve, a mining town of some size. At the present time I am more particularly' interested in the town of New Waterford. I intended writing to the department about the matter last summer, and now urge the minister to have his engineer in North Sydney look over the situation and make a report to his department as to the necessity of a public building, especially in view of the fact that the Minister of Customs has announced that he will establish a customs outport there.

If it is recommended by the Minister of Customs that there should 120i
be a customs house there, I shall be glad to have the inspector of public buildings visit the place and see if it is desirable to erect a building.

I would also wish to call attention to several towns in the constituency of Yarmouth. Wedgeport is an incorporated town of twenty-five hundred population. There is a customs office there and a large business is done in the fishing industry. Another village of quite large size is Tusket. Then there is Pubnico. There is still another in the north part of the county, Port Maitland. There are customs officers in all these places, goods are entered and duty paid. If it is the policy of the Government to spend money for public buildings in these smaller places- that is if they do not put the amounts in the Estimates and not expend them-but if they are put in there for the real purpose of erecting public buildings, I think it would be a good thing for these vill.age3 all over Nova Scotia, and I would commend the places I have named to the consideration of the Minister of Public Works.

Perhaps my case is more striking than any of those which have been mentioned. In the Estimates of 1912 there was an item of $3,000 for a public building at Port Hawkesbury, which has a population of between 1,500 and 2,000. This public building would have served not only the town of Hawkesbury but also Port Hastings, about a mile and a half distant, and Point Tupper, about three-quarters of a mile from Port Hawkesbury. The revenue of Hawkesbury post office is $1,690, which is a very substantial amount. This will form an index to the other data necessary to convince the minister. What surprises me in view of the fact that the hon. minister looks with favour upon the idea of putting a public building in Bear River-and I am not saying a word against Bear River, I hope they will get the public building-is that this item of $3,000 for a building at Hawkesbury should have been dropped. Anybody who has travelled on the Intercolonial railway cannot fail to have observed that the town of Hawkesbury is surrounded 'by a very progressive country district, and there are also several small towns in its neighbourhood. The late Government went further and showed its honesty of purpose by taking an option on a site for the building at Hawkesbury, and was getting the necessary documents made out when it was defeated in the election of 1911.

This goes to show that the late Government intended putting that building there, and in face of all these facts I think I am reasonable when I say I cannot understand why the matter has been dropped. However, I am in hopes that the hon. minister will look favourably upon the idea of having this item placed, with perhaps a couple of thousand more, in the Supplementary Estimates. I must express my surprise at finding that no effort has been made by friends of the present Government in Port Hawkesbury or Inverness to have this undertaking carried to a finish. The minister will have no trouble in getting a site, for the Government got an option on a very beautiful site, which might accommodate all the Government offices at Hawkesbury, and there are several.
I am surprised to hear that the item has been dropped. I will look into it and see what can be done.

I do not think the Government would ever place an item in the Estimates without having some idea of carrying out the work. As my hon. friend will remember, there was very considerable objection last year to spending much money in the county of Antigonish.

There was no objection on my part. I distinctly stated my hope that not only would the minister place the items in the Estimates, as he promised in that letter he wrote to Senator Girroir for political purposes, but that the money would be expended. I considered
the proposed expenditures to be proper and necessary. I regret to say that not one-quarter of the money promised on that occasion was voted, and not one-tenth of it has been expended.

There is also the additional reason, that the department cannot in one year, erect all the public buildings that are asked for in every part of the country. We have to get time to carry out the programme we have inaugurated and we are endeavouring to do so as well as we possibly can. If anything has been overlooked, so far as my hon. friend is concerned, we will try to remedy it. I would remind the hon. gentleman that the Department of Public Works is, in a sense, the pack horse for carrying on public buildings for all other departments of Government. As to the armoury, the hon. gentleman may be right about the site, because he lives hi the locality and understands the local conditions, and I shall be glad to draw to the attention of the Minister of Militia his statement, with the view of ascertaining if it is borne out by the information in the department.

It is the
statement of an officer of the department; it is not my statement.
Bridgetown public building, $4,000.
What is this vote for?

It is a re-vote for the
purchase of a site for the erection of a public building in Bridgetown, for a post office, etc. It was prayed for by the ratepayers and the Board of Trade, and was recommended by G. W. Pickup on May 10, 1911. There was gn appropriation of $4,000 for 1913, but nothing was expended. Bridgetown has a population of 1,000; it is a well-built, prosperous town, with a splendid surrounding country, and the people think they should have a public building to correspond with the buildings they have erected themselves.
Is there no public building there now?
No.
Bridgetown is certainly entitled to a building.

The population is about
1,000?
The official census of 1910 gave the population as 996.
That is wrong, it is more than that.
That is for the village itself.

The Minister of Public Works is taking a great interest in erecting public buildings in comparatively small towns, and I wish to draw his attention to an important shire town in the province of New Brunswick, which is without any public building. I refer to the town of Edmundston which has a (population of 2,000. It is an incorporated growing town. The post office revenue last year was $2,989, and the revenue from customs $32,000. There is paid in that town about $3,000 per week in wages to working people. The post office there now is rented for a few7 dollars a year, and the office of the collector of customs is in another building altogether. In view of these facts I ask the minister if it is not fair, that a town like Edmundston, through which the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Temiscouata railway and Canadian Pacific railway run, should have a public building. I know that the Minister of Public Works is very busy all the year around, but when he takes another flying trip to St. John, for the perfectly laudable purpose of helping his friend, the Minister of Marine, I hope he will find time to visit Edmundston, and we will give him a cordial welcome. We have any amount of work waiting for him in and around Edmundston, and if he visits us he will see the great necessity there is for these works. I hope that next summer we shall have the pleasure of seeing him up in that part, of the country. If he visits the town of Edmundston, I am sure we shall have a post office there within a year after his visit.	'

I appreciate the compliment of my hon. friend's invitation to visit the town of Edmundston. If it is possible for me to go there next summer, I shall be delighted to do so. If I go and find the conditions as thriving and as prosperous as my hon. friend suggests, I shall be equally delighted to lend what assistance I can to secure for that town a public building.

Do not strike
election time.
I am sorry that my hon. friend (Mr. Michaud) has not applied to me before.
The elections are not all over, I understand. Some are coming, and there is still time.

I would invite the
hon. gentleman to visit St. Jacques and see my post office.
Was not an amount of $15,000 voted for that post office?

$20,000, but it has
been dropped since. Perhaps the department will think proper to put it in again.

What is the estimated
cost of the building at Bridgetown, and has any site been bought?

A site has not yet been
bought. The plans have not yet been prepared. The rent paid is $200 and the postal revenue is $3,860.40. The customs duty collected is over $3,000; money orders, $28,000; money orders paid, $23,000; salary of the postmaster, $1,292; commission on money orders, $140; allowance for transfer of mails, $100. No estimate has as yet been made of the cost of the building.

What is
the reason for having that item in the Estimates of last year and again in the Estimates of this year, seeing that no estimate has been obtained of the cost of the work?
The simple answer to my hon. friend is that we had probably more work to do than we were able to attend to.

Would it not be better not to include these items in the Estimates? If there are no plans or specification or any arrangement for the construction of this building, would it not be better to drop this item?
I cannot agree with my hon. friend.

I think it is farcical to put in all these Estimates year after year and not have any work done. Some of this work should have been done. I notice that most of these items are revotes. We have no assurance that these items will not meet with the same fate this year as they met with last year. If they are to meet with the same fate this year, it is better to drop them altogether, as it is only holding out false hopes to the people.

There would be some reason for my hon. friend's statement if

we were proposing (to hold out any false hopes to the people at Bridgetown; but 1 assure my hon. friend that we are not doing so. From the .population and the postal business done in that (town, it is certainly a place entitled to a post office, and it will receive the early consideration of the department.
Canning public building, $5,000.
Will that complete the building?
What is the revenue there?

The postal revenue is '$1,195.52. The year before it was $2,017.99; money orders, $3,347; money orders paid, $11,403; salary of the postmaster, $805; commission on money orders, $124; allowance for transfer of mail, $74.
What is the population?
The population at the census of 1911 was 729.

I cannot find it in the
census.
It is given here in my report.
What is the cost of the site for this building?
There is a difficulty about it. We are proposing to expropriate a site.
What sum was offered by the department?
$2,000 I think.
Which was declined?

I believe so. We are
expropriating now.

From whom are you
buying the land?
Mr. N. W. Eaton and the Nova Scotia Produce and Supply Company, if that site is selected.

I asked for some papers in regard to the question of a site for this post office, and I am sorry that they have not been brought down prior to asking for this vote. I was advised some time ago, that when it was proposed by the department to erect a post office at Canning, a free site was offered to the department by Sir Frederick Borden, who is a resident of that town. Is that correct, and, if so, upon what ground has the offer been declined?

A free site was offered
iby Sir Frederick Borden to the town of Canning on condition that it should be made a post office site, but the offer was not directed to the Government, and the majority of the people of Canning did not approve of the site. That is the information I have received from my deputy.

What information , has the minister to the effect that the majority of the people of Canning do not wish to accept the site offered as the location for the post office? How did that intelligence come to the department?

My hon. friend asked for this information and I happened to 'be looking at it to-day, but I had not time to go into it. I shall be glad to allow the item to stand1 until I bring down the papers, because I am desirous of giving all the information possible.
I am not desirous that the item should stand over, because I presume I shall have another opportunity of discussing the matter if I think it necessary.

Certainly, and I will
bring down the papers as soon as I can.

I am told that Sir
Frederick Borden offered this Government a free site for this proposed public building at Canning, and I am sure that he would not offer a free site unless it was one eminently suited for such a purpose, because there is hardly another man living in Canning who has given evidence of such public interest in his home town as has Sir Frederick Borden. I have not the slightest doubt that the site is in every respect suitable. The minister intimates that the site offered by Sir Frederick Borden was not deemed suitable by the citizens of the town. He has intimated that the majority of the citizens of Canning in some way expressed their disapproval of it. I think we should know just the nature of this protest-
That is what 1 say: I shall be glad to bring down the information.

-and how it came here. I should be very suspicious that there is but little foundation that the site offered was not a suitable one. I have some little knowledge of the site which Sir Frederick Borden offered, and I should think it would be a much better site than the one now proposed to be taken, Now, in connection with the site proposed to be taken, I under-

stand that the department had made an offer to one of the owners-Mr. Eaton, is it not?-and to the Nova Scotia Produce and Supply Company. Is it correct that the Nova Scotia Produce and Supply Company declined the offer the department made for their interest in this site on the ground that the offer was too large?

The deputy informs me
that there is nothing in our records to show that, and I have never heard of it before.
Is not the land proposed to be taken for this site owned by Sir Frederick Borden?

The deputy informs me
that he understands that is Sir Frederick Borden's company.
And has the department no information from that company that they declined to accept the offer of the department on the ground that it was too much for the land?

The deputy informs me
he has none, and certainly I have none. But as my hon. friend has asked for the papers, I would rather allow this item to stand and bring them all down.
Chester public building, $25,000.

What is the population of
Chester according to the information of the hon. minister.
In 1911 it was 1,096.

I have here the census for 1911, and I find that the population of Chester Corner is 418; Chester Basin, 357; Chester East, 425; and Chester West, 528. These are four polling subdivisions, and, of course, a public building erected in any one of them would not accommodate the others. The district is fifteen miles long. I suppose the polling subdivision in which thje building is being put is Chester Basin, is it not ? It seems to me the minister is * going some ' when he undertakes to erect public buildings in villages such as this. And this also, is a re-vote. I confess I have some doubt as to the bona fides of some person with respect to the expenditure of this money, that doubt being based on the reception given to proposals made by the late Government to erect public buildings in very much larger communities by hon. gentlemen who now support the ministry, but who were then in Opposition. I assume that their opposition in those days was sincere and well intended. That being so, 
they certainly cannot have executed such an extraordinary change of front as to give support to the expenditure of money in very much smaller communities. I would ask also if the minister would tell the committee the postal and customs revenue from the village in which this public building is to be erected.

The postal revenue is #1,862.36; money orders, #48,605.35; money orders paid, $15,558.09; postmaster's income: salary, $755; commission on money orders, $131; savings bank, $40; postal notes, #10; allowance for transference of mail, $4. I do not appear to have anything with respect to the Customs.
What rental is being paid now by the Post Office Department ?
One hundred dollars.

How much was
paid for the site ?
An Order in Council was passed securing the site for $2,250.
From whom ?
Airs. Florence Manning.
Are we to understand that the total expenditure will be $25,000?
Yes.

I submit that that is a
pretty large sum to expend for a public building in the village of Chester, which, according to the census return has a population of about 400.
The census returns show 1,096.

I know the minister has
figures that indicate that population. But as I pointed out, that includes three polling subdivisions covering territory of a total length of about fifteen miles. Tne minister would not pretend to this committee that this post office building is going to accommodate this whole territory. There are probably eight or ten post offices in that area. Therefore, when I venture the statement that this building, which is to cost $25,000, will only accommodate a population of about 400, I am stating what is absolutely within the mark.

I know that
the hon. gentleman does not wish to make a mistatement. But I have before me the census returns and they show that Chester West has a population of 1,096, Chester East 850, Chester Basin 624. I do not believe the hon. gentleman can have the

proper returns before him or he would not make the statement he does.

That does not
afford the information; I know the district well.

But this post office will not
serve all these places.

But the one
in which this building is to be erected has a population of 1,096, as given by the minister.

There cannot be any question as to the sort of community that this twenty-five thousand dollar public building is intended to serve. Those of us who represent constituencies in Nova Scotia know full well that the public buildings contemplated by this vote will only serve a very small portion of the population set down as belonging to the district of Chester, in the county of Lunenburg.
It must be borne in mind that Chester >s not an incorporated town or village; it is simply a polling subdivision. During the summer months a large number of people from the United States visit that district, which is a popular summer resort for tourists. Outside of that, the population is extremely sparse. I did not raise any very great objection to the vote of $4,000 for the erection of a public building at Bear River; the amount of the vote is not very large, but in asking this committee to vote $25,000 to erect a public building in the village of Chester, I think the hon. minister is asking more than he can reasonably expect the committee to accede to.
There is nothing here to show that this is a revote.

It was understood to be a revote. I would suggest that the item pass at $25,000.
Dartmouth-New public building, $40,000.
Has a site been purchased for this building?

Yes. This amount is to be used towards the erection of a new building at Dartmouth, on the site authorized to be expropriated by Order in Council dated August 30, 1913, situated on the corner of Burrell and Wentworth streets, to replace the present building, which is entirely inadequate to the large and growing post office needs of the town.
How much was paid for the site?

To Turner estate, $2,500;
J. F. Leahy, $2,900; Jacob Tynes, $2,900.

A new post office is very much needed in the town of Dartmouth because the capacity of the present building is altogether inadequate. This sum of money has been voted, I think, for a considerable number of years, and I would like to urge upon the minister the desirability of asking for tenders for the building so that it may be erected as soon as possible.
Only a short time ago we closed the negotiations for the site; plans are now being prepared and we will go ahead with it immediately.

On two or three' occasions this evening the minister was asked for the population of certain districts to be served by proposed post offices, and in reply the minister gave the population furnished by some of his officials. I would point out that the information thus given is altogether misleading. It is of no assistance whatever to take up the census returns and produce therefrom the population of certain districts, as the information thus obtained may be of no use. In the case of two votes passed this evening for public buildings in Nova Scotia the populations given by the minister referred to areas within which there were probably a dozen or more post offices, and only a very small part of those sections would be served by the proposed post offices. I refer to this not for the purpose of criticising, but merely to urge upon the minister that hereafter the officers of the department should furnish him with information which is correct and which will supply the information desired by the committee. This could easily be obtained by the post office inspector or the local postmasters in the province of Nova Scotia. Any statement of population should include only the number of residents within the district or territory to be served by the proposed post office.
Fort Cumberland (Fort Beausejour)-res-toration, $5,000.

This is an institution which has (been almost entirely forgotten in the province of Nova Scotia. It is a thing of ancient history, and so far as the passer-by is concerned, there is nothing to be seen. I would like to know what reports the engineer of the department has made with regard to this matter, and what public interests are to be served by this

expenditure. There are a great many things in Nova Scotia that need the expenditure of money much more than this, any expenditure in connection with which would serve a much better purpose than the restoration of this old forgotten fort.

This vote was given to us by the Militia Department, and does not carry with it very much explanation. I shall be glad to allow the item to stand until the Minister of Militia is here and can give us the reason why the vote has been recommended.
Item stands.
Glace Bay public building-repairs, etc., $1,500.
Is not that a revote?
No, that is a new vote.
What are the proposed improvements?

To point the brickwork, including staging, $645; to paint outside woodwork, window frames and sashes, 375; kalsomining all the interior walls and ceilings, $150; two pairs of double outside doors, $80; to provide gates on each side of the building, $50; heating, $100; contingencies, $400; total, $1,500.
Halifax citadel-New quarters for single men and recreation establishment, $15,000.

There is no objection to this item, (but it is along the same line as the matter of which I spoke prior to the House rising at six o'clock. This is along the same line of military expenditure. I know that the Minister of Public Works is an extremely peaceful man.
He was not last night.

He always is, even my
hon. friend from Cape Breton to the contrary notwithstanding. The military expenditure in the Dominion I believe is vastly greater than is really approved of by the people of Canada. It appears to me that the war lord we have at present at the head of military affairs is entirely exceeding what really ought to be done in this country. I wish to read to the committee, from the Montreal Daily Star of Friday, March 20, 1914, a cablegram signed Windermere, in which the correspondent says:
The Yorkshire Post says the Hon. Colonel Sam. Hughes has informed the Orange organizations that the Canadian Government propose to take no action to prevent the departure of [Hr. McKenzie.]
the first contingent of one thousand picked Canadian Orangemen who are coming to Belfast in May next.
Windermere.
Undoubtedly, I take it, that is in connection with the Home Rule agitation. It appears that the activities of the war lord at present at the head of our militia department are so large, so strong, and so exuberant, that he cannot confine them even to the Dominion of 'Canada. I would suggest to the Minister of Public Works and the Postmaster General-who is pacific at times, but not at all times as the Minister of Public Works is-that he ought to take a hand in this proposition and curtail the powers of speech and of action of the Minister of Militia and Defence; take him aside in a fatherly way and say to him that in the management of the Canadian militia there is quite enough for a man even of his ability to attend to in this country without meddling in outside propositions. I think it would be well for the Government, and I am bound to say I think it would be remarkably well for the people of Canada, if the Government would take the hon. the Minister of Militia aside and just say to him that we have a good deal of business to attend to in this country ourselves, and that perhaps Great Britain is quite able to take care of her own affairs; that it would be well for the minister to look after what he has to look after, if he only would, and leave outside matters alone.	.

My hon. friend is probably assuming more than he usually assumes by accepting a statement in a newspaper clipping as being absolutely correct and as representing the words of the Minister of Militia. I do not think my hon. friend would desire to do the minister an injustice by quoting a statement appearing in a newspaper as being an authoritative statement emanating from the Minister of Militia without having the word of the minister himself.

The remarks of the
Minister of Public Works may be very well taken, but the Minister of Militia, when these items are going through, ought to be here to answer for himself and tell us whether or not any such intimation has gone from him. In the meantime, all we have is the word of the Minister of Public Works, which of course I am prepared at all times to accept, that he does not know whether this has been said or not. But the Montreal Star is strongly in the confidence

'of the Government, and this comes very authentically.
What would you do with him if he did say so?

I would suggest that we postpone any items having reference to the minister's department until the Minister of Militia and Defence has sufficiently recovered from the recent engagement to be able to come to the House and make a statement himself. Notwithstanding the fact that our friend the Minister of Public Works is inclined to treat with some lightness the serious information contained in the Montreal Star, I am bound to say that in view of frequent rumours that have been sent abroad from the centre of military operations here on Parliament Hill with regard to the attitude of certain high officials on this important question which is agitating Great Britain at the present time,
I am inclined to think there is perhaps too much ground for the cable despatch which the hon. member for Lambton has read. It is a fact that a serious crisis has been reached in the old country and I am quite sure that the action of the Minister of Militia and Defence in giving expression to utterances such as he has given in the past, is not calculated to allay that feeling and as one member of the Canadian Parliament I certainly think that it is our duty to refuse to vote any sum for military purposes in Canada until we have had an opportunity of hearing from the Minister of Militia himself whether or not these assertions and rumours have any ground. Yesterday we had information in this House that another important member of this Government assisted, or at all events was a party to a delegation which had anything but a peaceful purpose in making a certain presentation to Sir Edward Carson on the eve of his departure for Ulster. It may be that the hon. gentlemen who form this ministry are not averse to having it known that they strongly sympathize with the gentlemen in the north of Ireland in resisting civil authority in the old country, but I venture to say that a very large proportion of the people of this country and a strong public opinion will not support them in the nostile stand they are taking against law and order. I would like the Minister of Public Works and every other member of this Government to take these matters a little more seriously when they are referred to in the House and to realize
for a moment that the sympathy which they are supposed to give and no doubt honestly intend to give shall not be given so generously until, at all events, we know what this crisis in the old country is going to result in.

What makes me nervous is that red hand offered to Sir Edward Carson when the Hon. Mr. Cochrane was present. It is not the sword-I do not think Sir Edward Carson will ever use it, in spite of all the threats he has made-but that red hand, really makes me nervous. Now, this notice given by Colonel Sam. Hughes, Minister of Militia, that a thousand picked men will soon leave for Belfast is a very serious matter, especially after the declaration made by several grand masters of Orange lodges. To show that there is a connection between all these facts, the hon. member for Westmorland read the other day a notice sent to the Yeomanry of Westmorland county: 'A call to Arms.' Certainly there is something going wrong.
There is corroboration.

Certainly there is corroboration-the presence of the hon. Mr. Cochrane at the presentation to Sir Edward Carson, the possibility of the departure of a thousand men from Canada for Ulster, and the call to arms in Westmorland. Certainly all this means war, very imminent war at that.

I did not intend to take part in the discussion of the Nova Scotia Estimates, but in view of the fact that this question has come up-and I do not mean to treat it seriously at all, for I do not think it is worthy of any serious treatment-I would ask the Minister of Public Work9 if Colonel Sam. Hughes did make the statement that he is supposed to have made, as published in the Yorkshire Post. Was he authorized by the Government to make that statement?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is wandering from the item under discussion.

I am not going any farther. What is bothering me is the fact that the Minister of Militia went a little further towards Ulster. I do not propose to follow him at all. I am simply asking the Minister of Public Works, was the Minister of Militia authorized by the Government to make that statement, and would the Government authorize the Minister of Militia

to send these men abroad, presumably to Ulster? I would like an answer.

In the first place let me say to my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) that I am a little disappointed in him for so frankly acknowledging that he was a little nervous by reason of the rumours of wars. I did not think he was a man to become nervous under any circumstances.
It is a case of Ulsteria.

I am rather surprised that our friends opposite should take up a simple report appearing in a newspaper without first hearing from the minister who is credited with the statements made, which I am sure every hon. gentleman well knows he would not make. So far as the item under discussion is concerned, there is no objection to allowing any item to stand in order that hon. gentlemen shall have all the information that can be given, but this is an item in respect to a citadel in Halifax of which the hon. member for Halifax approves. There are several other items, any of which could stand, if hon. gentlemen desire it, in order to get an answer from the Minister of Militia.
Would the minister give us an assurance that none of this money proposed to be voted will be used against the Crown, honour and dignity of His Majesty the King.
I would prefer the minister to be here. I would like him to explain the quarrel with the officers at that dinner.

We will let the drill hall item stand.
Halifax Customs examining warehouse $100,000. '
Where is that to be built; has a site been purchased?
It is to be built, I understand, on the Euel Yard property.
The Government owns that site?
The Imperial Government owns it, but we are making arrangements to get it.
Will you get the title?
Yes, so the deputy minister informs me.
Is the looation approved of by the business men of Halifax? It strikes me that perhaps it is not too convenient a situation. However, 10 p.m. I am not in a position to say that it is not a good site.

There has been no
objection to it.
Halifax-Postal station at north end, $55,000.
This is for a post office in the north end of the city of Halifax?
Yes.
Has a site been purchased? If so, from whom? Where is it located, and what does it cost?

The site has a united frontage of 60 feet on Gottingen street, and a depth of 100 feet along Prince William street. An Order in Council was passed on the 16th February, 1914, to purchase from Mr. F. W. Hanright for the sum of $7,000-which amount includes the building on the properties-parcels A and B on plan accompanying Order in Council having respectively the following dimensions: A, 68 feet by 30 feet; B, 60 feet by 31 feet 6 inches; and to expropriate parcel C (68 feet by 30 feet) on plan accompanying Order in Council, and to tender for the .same the sum of $8,294, which amount is to include the buildings on the property. This parcel is owned by Matilda Mason, wife of John J. Mason.
Were any other sites offered to the department ?
A number of sites were examined. The Postmaster General informs me that this site was selected by the post office inspector who went down there for that purpose.
By the post office inspector of Nova Scotia ?
No, the chief inspector. He informs me it is necessary to have a postal station at that point.
Will the building be proceeded with this year ? Are tenders to be invited ?
Yes.
What will be the cost V Mr. ROGERS: About $70,000 or $80,000
The site was purchased from Mr. Hanright for $7,000.
Yes.
I wonder if it is a mere coincidence that Mr. Hanright is an oft-defeated candidate in Nova Scotia ? Or is it because this particular property has special merits as a post office site P
It had the recommendation of the chief inspector of the Post Office Department, who is a very old and trustworthy servant.
Has the minister any information as to what Mr. Hanright paid for the site ?
No.
Or as to how long he held the property before transferring it to the Government ?
No information.
Has the site been actually transferred to the department ?
The deputy minister informs me that the Justice Department is working on it.
The transfer has not been actually made ?

Apparently not.
Halifax-Quarantine station on Lawior's island, $25,000.
What is this for ?

This is a re-vote of $25,000 for the erection of new buildings and improvement of existing buildings on Lawior's island. The estimated cost of a laboratory is $7,000; residence for medical bacteriologist, $10,000, and for medical superintendent, $10,000; residence for captain, $4,000; well, painting, &c.,	$5,500;
building at rear of bath to be used as dressing room, sheeted and painted, $575; plank passage-way from above building to rear of disinfection building, $80; coachhouse, $425; contingencies and superintendence, $9,535, and residence for engineer, $2,500.

The medical
superintendent is supposed to reside at the quarantine station?
Yes.

When we are
voting money for buildings which are to be used by the Department of Agriculture, or by the Department of Militia, the ministers of these departments should be here to give explanations. They should take charge, at least up to the voting of the money.

The practice has been
for the Department of Public Works to take charge of such votes.

A great many people
think that Lawior's island is the wrong place for the quarantine station; but I suppose it is hardly worth discussing that, when the Minister of Agriculture, who has charge of quarantine matters, is absent.

How long has it been the
custom to place the votes for armouries and drill halls under the Public Works Department?
The chief architect tells me it has been the custom for a great many years.

I was informed recently, in
reply to a question, that two and a half million dollars' worth of armouries and drill halls, to be constructed by the Public Works Department, would be transferred to the Militia Department. I never could understand why these votes should not be placed in the Militia Estimates, so that the minister would be here to give us explanations. An application was made for an armoury in Yarmouth, and the Minister of Militia promised the representative of the boosters' club of that town that the armoury would be built during the coming season, but there is no vote for it in the Estimates.

Another strong
reason why the Minister of Militia should be here is that he informed Parliament a session or two ago that the Militia Department could build these drill halls much better and much cheaper than could the Public Works Department. In view of that the suggestion is worth considering.

When items
concerning buildings for quarantine or militia are under consideration, the ministers of these departments should be here. I want to get information about a drill hall in Inverness, which was provided for by the late Government, but it is not reasonable to expect the Minister of Public WorkB to give me that information; the Minister of Militia should be here.

The Minister of Militia
will be here when we take up these Estimates on the next occasion, and the

hon. gentleman will have opportunity to get the information.
It will be understood that although we pass these items for militia buildings, hon. gentlemen who desire information with regard to them will be entitled to get it later.
Absolutely.

We are not anxious to
delay the Estimates in any way, but I think this request is reasonable.

There will be no objection to that taken at any time.
Hantsport public building, $4,000.

What will this
building cost?
We have no plans yet.

In the remarks 1 am' going to make, I have not in my mind any public building which it is proposed to build in Nova Scotia, but still I feel that a protest should be made against the construction of unnecessarily expensive buildings for post office purposes, in my own province or in any other province. If it is necessary to erect a public building in a village or small town, well and good, but if $10,000 will give the requisite accommodation, it is highly improper to expend $25,000 or $40,000. I think the minister will agree with me in that. There are many public buildings throughout Nova Scotia, which did not cost more than $25,000 or $30,000 in towns of 4,000 or 5,000 population, and I notice a tendency to erect buildings of equal cost in towns of two or three hundred inhabitants, and where the revenue is very limited. It is very easy for the political advisers of the minister to, impose upon him, but in the erection of those buildings throughout Canada, he should exercise the most careful personal supervision. It is very difficult for a minister to resist such an application, and it is impossible for him to meet all the demands, but nevertheless, when he does accede to a request, he should exercise care with respect to the cost. There are many cases, in my own province for instance, where buildings are proposed which will cost $25,000 or $30,000, and where, in my judgment, it is absolutely unnecessary and a waste of public money to expend so much.
I think in most cases the localities interested would be satisfied with more modest and less expensive buildings.

I am very glad that my hon. friend (Mr. A. K. Maclean) has brought up this question, because I am disposed to agree with him in a very great measure. I may say, for the information of the committee, that I have had a very serious discussion with the chief architect and those associated with him, pointing out exactly what my hon. friend has suggested, namely, that we must get to a reasonable cost if we are going to erect buildings in towns such as that now under discussion. My own idea is, that the department should not undertake the erection of public buildings in a town that has not at least a population of 1,000. I am trying to lay it down as a hard and fast rule, if I can possibly carry it out, that for a town of that size we should not expend in a public building a larger amount than $12,000 or $15,000. The chief architect has had definite instructions in preparing plans from now on in respect to such buildings. We are endeavouring to have a standard plan to meet conditions of that kind in order that there will be a similarity in the different towns of those sizes, and that the town that will get a better building will have to have a larger population than the town that is at a lower grade. We are adopting this plan and intend to enforce it as strictly as possible.

In many cases it would be much cheaper for the department to pay rental than to build public buildings. A few years ago in my town I advised the department to rent a building which was constructed for a bank and a post office. The department told me that it was not its practice to do so. I convinced the minister that it was cheaper for the department to do that than to build a building. The vminister acceded to my request and the department is paying only $125 a year, but the postmaster gets also the rent allowance allowed by the Post Office Department of about $75 a year, making altogether an expenditure of $200 a year. The department has not the maintenance of any building nor any salary of a caretaker to pay. In many small towns the department -would find good buildings erected.
In many cases we rent buildings.
Has the land not been purchased yet for this building?

In thickly
settled districts, especially in the province of Ontario-and it must be much the same

in Nova Scotia

since the rural mail routes have been established, out of many of the towns are running six or eight or possibly ten rural mail routes, and possibly eight or ten offices in the surrounding country have been closed during the last few years. Consequently the mail that is being distributed from even a small centre has increased so much that it is important in many of the small districts that reasonable room should be given for the post office.

I am very glad to hear the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) speaking on rural mail routes. They must be far more plentiful in Ontario than in Nova Scotia. There are very few mail routes in, the county of Yarmouth and the postmaster has not seen fit to grant them yet.
There are plenty in Ontario.	I

Rural mail routes are established for anybody who wants to have them.
Middleton public building, $15,000.
From whom was the site for this building bought?

The site was purchased on the I8th of December, 1912, from Fred. E. Bently, James A. Gates, John H. Hall and T. A. Croker, for the sum of $2,500.
North Sydney public building-Improvements, $5,000.

For some time I have been endeavouring to get information from the department regarding some work done on the public building at North Sydney. How much money has been expended on this building during the last two years?
The deputy says that we have not got that information here, but I shall be glad to supply it when our Estimates come up again.
Is this item for payment of work already done or for work in prospect?

The vote of $5,000 is to provide for an addition to be built in the rear of the North Sydney public building for an examining warehouse, so that the room now used may be given to the postoffice, and the front porch is to give more room in lobby. The addition for examining warehouse, 20 x 25 feet, $2,500; front porch, 25 x 8 feet, altering windows,
$1,500; town clock and installation, $1,000, make a total estimated cost of $5,000.

I wish to know whether the expenditures on that building for the last year were by tender and contract. If so, who were the tenderers and which was the lowest tender? I understand that there was some loss by fire on that building during the construction of the work and that new tenders were asked or that the work was commenced over again. The work was nearly finished before the fire broke out and very slight damage was done. The work was done over again or a similar amount given for the work the second time as was given for it the first time. Were tenders called for on the second occasion, as well as on the first occasion? If the work was inspected I would like to have a report of the inspector who supervised the work. As far as this vote is concerned, I am pleased to hear that the minister is going to restore the vote, for 'the installation of the clock. That is an old vote; it was dropped last year. I spoke to the minister about it and I am very glad that he has restored it. There were two other votes for a similar purpose in my riding. There are three public buildings in my riding, one in the shire town, one in the town of Sydney Mines, and the other in the town of North Sydney. Before the present Government came into power, there were votes to install a clock on each of these buildings. This was no special favour for these buildings, because I understood from officials of the department that it was rather the policy, particularly in the province of Nova Scotia, to have a clock on each of the public buildings belonging to the department. Those items were all dropped at the change of gover.-ment. Can the minister tell me if he is going to install a clock at Baddeck, and a clock in the town of Sydney Mines?

I have not the information before me at the moment; but we will come to it later on, and I shall be glad to give my hon. friend the information.
Sydney Mines public buildings-Improvements, repairs, etc., $2,500.

This vote is to make provision for purchasing and installing a clock in the tower of the Sydney Mines public building at an estimated cost of $1,000, and repairs and improvements to the building, $1,500.

I am pleased to find
this vote in the Estimates. But I notice

there is nothing for Baddeck. That is the shire town of Victoria and there is a public building there. There was a vote made at the same time as the other for Baddeck. but that has been dropped. Seeing the minister has been good enough to restore the other two votes, I hope he will remember Baddeck in the Supplementary Estimates. A clock would be quite an ornament to the building and a very good thing for the town.

I think my hon. friend
has been very lucky in getting two out of three; he must not hurry too much; we are doing the best we can.

Why make two bites of a cherry?
Truro-New public building, $40,000.
What is to be the cost of this building?
We have entirely outgrown the old building there. The chief architect thinks that the cost will be $50,000.

Is this a new building, or
improvements and extensions?
It is to purchase a site and erect a new building.
How much will the land cast?
We have not got it yet. The population of Truro is over 6,000. The town is growing, and a larger public building is urgently needed.

I cut a piece out of the
Yarmouth Herald, of one of the issues of February last, and perhaps by reading this I can shorten the remarks I have to make on this subject:	-
Building Post Offices that are not Wanted.
As an evidence or the shameful wastefulness of the present Tory Government at Ottawa and its unfairness in dealing with the necessities of the public, we may cite the case of the appropriation of $140,000 for a new post office building for Truro, $40,000 of which is in the Estimates for the present year.
As the chief architect says that the cost will be $50,000, that is probably an error.
Truro has a more up-to-date post office than has Yarmouth, and although not quite as large is adequate for the necessities of the town. Truro, not being a seaport town, of course, does not require so large accommodation for such offices as harbour-master, shipping-master and others.
To show how the people of Truro view the appropriation the News of Monday last has a letter from Mr. C. P. Blanchard, a former official, who writes:
To those who are not acquainted with exist-

ing conditions this may seem to be a necessary expenditure, but to those who are best informed in the matter it is a needless extravagance and waste of public money. Some two years ago the Government architect visited the Truro post office, and together we made a careful survey of the building and the additional requirements to make it up to date in every particular, and the decision arrived at was that an addition to the rear of the present building for a forwarding department and other improvements, to cost in all not more than $10,000, would give a post office and custom house ample for the requirements of a town such as Truro for a period of at least twenty-five years. There is no question that within a very few years we will have mail delivery by carriers, which will greatly lessen the space required in the post office for private boxes, and consequently give more space for other work if needed. There are a dozen other ways in which this appropriation can be expended which will be of greater value to the town than a new post office, the erection of which in the opinion of the writer would be entirely wrong.'
This is from a former employee of the Post Office Department.
What became of him?

I suppose he was dismissed by the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier); he is probably among the 1,200 officials whom that hon. gentleman has beheaded. The Herald goes on:
There is an absolute necessity for a new building in Yarmouth, and the delay attendant upon the matter is not only an outrage upon our people, but is a political scandal. There is no excuse for it. The authorities, from the minister down, are aware of our necessities, and there is no reason, except downright neglect or partisanship, that delays the work. How long is it to continue?
I agree entirely with the remarks of this newspaper. Last year I brought" the needs of Yarmouth to the attention of the Minister of Public Works, and he told me that he would take the matter into consideration. I waited until the Estimates came down this year, but there was not a dollar for the enlargement of the public building there, nor in the Supplementary Estimates. Yarmouth is a larger place than Truro. Our customs revenue is reaching nearly to the hundred-thousand-dollar mark. Yarmouth is destined to grow very much more in the future than in the past. The accommodation in our public building at Yarmouth is altogetiier inadequate for the po3t office requirements. There are times, especially during the holidays, when the people have to stand on the sidewalk, whatever the weather may be, and wait for their turn to get into the post office. I presented this matter to the former Admin-

istration, and I am happy to say that after examining into it they purchased a building directly south of the present building for which they paid $10,000, and when the old Government went out there was an item in the Estimates to remodel that building and enlarge the accommodation. But since the present Government came into power that building has been standing there as a monumental disgrace to the Government and an insult to the people of Yar-moutn. It is the great centre for the display of the circus and moving-picture show bills, but that is all. If the Government do not intend to enlarge the post office premises why do not they rent the building? It would rent for $1,000 or $1,200 a year, for there is a fine large store on the ground floor and there are offices on the floor above. Yet it is left vacant. I submit that a town of the importance of Yarmouth is entitled to better consideration than this by the present Government. Though for some years they have not sent a man to Parliament in accord with the party now in power, yet I hold that the people of Yarmouth are entitled to fair and decent treatment in regard to the finances of Canada. They contribute very largely and I consider that under the circumstances the Minister of Public Works should have a vote in the Supplementary Estimates to enlarge that building. I am sure that if he submitted the matter to his friends there, to the patronage committee of Yarmouth, they would recommend that that building be immediately enlarged so that the post office would have room for its work and the public would be furnished with a decent place to stand in while transacting post office business. That kind of treatment would be all right fifty years ago, or if accorded to a backwoods settlement, but Yarmouth is tsufficiently important to deserve better treatment from the present Government than it has received in connection with this matter.

I- do not rise to speak particularly about the post office at Yarmouth, as I have never had the pleasure of being in that town, but in justice to Truro I think my hon. friend might try to get what he wants without running down Truro. I have been in Truro, and I made a point to speak to the hon. Minister of Public Works with a view to securing better post office accommodation for that town. Truro is an important railway centre and divisional point, and its post office 121
accommodation is absolutely inadequate. There is no doubt that the $40,000 will be spent there, so the paper to which my hon. friend has referred is misleading the public in the matter. The former official of the department whose name my hon. friend has given, does not know what he is talking about when he says that there is to be distribution of mail by carriers in Truro, and that consequently the needs of the post office will be lessened. When you have letter carriers in a town or city you have to enlarge the post office and provide additional accommodation for them. My hon. friend can rest assured that what is being done for Truro is absolutely justifiable, and that this vote is a perfectly legitimate expenditure.

I was not running down Truro at all; I was simply placing before the Committee the views of Mr. Blanchard, a former employee of the Post Office Department there, and advocating the same treatment for Yarmouth as that which is being accorded to Truro. If the hon. Postmaster General will look at the papers in his department in connection with this matter, he will find that the chief inspector has several times reported on the inadequacy of the Yarmouth post office. I hope what I have said about the needs of Yarmouth in this regard may bring forth fruit; perhaps the Minister of Public Works may have a contingent fund out of which he can provide for the necessary expenditure. For the sum of $15,000 the present building could be enlarged. The amount needed is not very great', and I think Yarmouth is entitled to that expenditure.
I will look the matter up to-morrow.

I submit that the
necessity for providing extra accommodation in the post office at North Sydney is brought about toy the transmission of mails through that post office which should not go there at all. I refer to the mails which are sent from Halifax to St. Pierre and Miquelon. This mail is first hauled to the train at Halifax; then it goes to North Sydney, where it is taken off the train and put in the post office, remaining there, perhaps, for days at a time; then it is trucked from the post office and put upon a boat which carries it to St. Pierre. I could never understand why that mail is not put on board the boat at Halifax and carried direct to St. Pierre and Miquelon.

It does not get there any quicker by being left at North Sydney; there is no advantage to the people of St. Pierre and Miquelon; why should this mail not be sent direct to its destination, thus avoiding its being piled in the post office at North Sydney, where there is no room for it. If that were done, the extra accommodation that is to be provided for the post office at North Sydney would not be required, because the room that is now taken up by this mail would be available to the staff of the post office for other purposes. I wish to bring this matter particularly to the attention of the Postmaster General, and I hope that he may take whatever steps are necessary to do away with the trouble experienced in this regard by the officials of the post office at North Sydney.

My hon. friend, being a resident of the place, probably understands the local conditions much better than any one else here. All I can say is that the representations which he has made will be submitted through ' Hansard ' to the officer of the department who is in charge of the management and despatch of the mails. If his representations carry any weight with them, I am sure that they will receive the careful and considerate attention of those in charge.
Tignish public building, $11,000.
What are the details of this expenditure?

This is a vote of $3,000, for a tower clock; $2,000 and $1,000 for sidewalks in connection with municipal undertakings around the building.
